Addition of the score to the basic clinical model yielded a category-free NRI of 0.27 (95% CI: 0.14-0.40; p < 0.001) and an IDI of 0.068 (95% CI: 0.035-0.101; p < 0.001), indicating improved apparent risk separation within the derivation cohort. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses showed a stepwise increase in mortality risk across score groups (HR: 3.12 for high-risk group, p < 0.001). Calibration and decision-curve analyses suggested favorable apparent model performance and potential net benefit within the present study cohort.

CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective single-center cohort, the composite score integrating NLR, albumin, and D-dimer was associated with 1-year mortality and showed promising apparent discriminatory performance. The score should be considered an exploratory prognostic tool that may complement comprehensive clinical assessment and support future risk-stratification research. Prospective multicenter studies with external validation and evaluation of clinical impact are required before its use in routine practice can be considered.

articles.title: Closed reduction in distal radius fractures: manual manipulation vs. finger trap traction-a prospective randomized controlled clinical trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Initial treatment of distal radius fractures (DRF) can be either performed without reduction or with a reduction method as finger-trap traction (FTT) only or by additional manual reduction (MR) under hematoma block. There is no clear evidence on which reduction method is superior, however, MR is more invasive and seems to lead to higher pain levels and more post reduction complications. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical relevance of MR compared to FTT in acute DRFs.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Study design was a prospective, single-centre, balanced randomized [1:1], and parallel grouped, controlled trial. Inclusion criteria were patients with a DRF type A2, A3 or C according to the AO classification and a dorsal tilt of ≥ 10°. The patients were randomized either in the FTT or in the MR group. Depending on the patient's functional demand and the fracture configuration, conservative or operative treatment was initiated. Over one year, clinical and radiological data were assessed at six follow-ups.

RESULTS: A total of 53 patients were included. Regarding radiological results neither FTT nor MR achieved sufficient reduction results (median dorsal tilt was - 16 to -18 after one year) and none of the techniques was superior. The clinical results between the conservatively treated groups were comparable and showed no significant difference. Complications included one CRPS in the conservative MR group, one CRPS after FTT and operation, one secondary carpal tunnel syndrome in the conservative FTT group and one skin lesion after MR.

CONCLUSION: Manual reduction under haematoma block showed no benefit. In patients with AO type A2, A3 and type C fractures and a dorsal tilt ≥ 10° only FTT (if required under a haematoma block or comparable analgesia) is recommended regardless of whether surgery is performed or not.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I randomized controlled trial.

TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07697976, registered 06/22/2026, retrospectively registered, www.

CLINICALTRIALS: gov .

articles.title: Coronal alignment-related mediolateral load distribution and polyethylene wear in a medial-pivot total knee arthroplasty design.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: While mechanical alignment in total knee arthroplasty aims for a neutral hip-knee-ankle angle, kinematic alignment preserves the native joint line, often allowing residual varus or valgus. Clinically, constitutional variations in alignment affect the coronal joint moments and the mediolateral load distribution, but the impact on polyethylene wear remains unclear.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Wear of a medial pivot total knee arthroplasty insert (MS 5C®, implantcast GmbH, Germany) was evaluated in a knee wear simulator replicating the walking cycle. Inserts were tested under three conditions representing overall lower-limb coronal alignment and the associated mediolateral load distribution: neutral (60% medial / 40% lateral), varus (70% / 30%), and valgus (50% / 50%), with three (n = 3) dynamically loaded inserts and one load-soak control per condition. Testing followed ISO 14243-1:2009 over 5 million cycles. Gravimetric wear and wear patterns were assessed.

RESULTS: A numerical trend was observed among the groups: The varus-related load distribution demonstrated the lowest overall wear (4.83 ± 1.06 mg/million cycles), whereas the valgus group produced the highest wear (9.43 ± 1.47 mg/million cycles); the neutral group was intermediate (6.81 ± 3.07 mg/million cycles). However, these differences did not reach statistical significance. Visual inspection revealed medial-dominant wear in all groups, with increased lateral wear under valgus-related load distribution.

CONCLUSIONS: Overall lower-limb coronal alignment and the associated mediolateral load distribution appear to influence polyethylene wear in total knee arthroplasty. The observed numerical trend suggests that alignment-related changes in mediolateral load distribution may influence polyethylene wear patterns in this medial-pivot TKA design. Further studies are required to determine the clinical relevance of these observations.

articles.title: Novel bicolumnar fixation with primary cup implantation for pelvic discontinuity in revision hip arthroplasty: a comparative clinical study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelvic discontinuity is a rare but challenging condition in revision hip arthroplasty. Traditional cage-based reconstruction techniques often rely solely on mechanical fixation and may be associated with implant migration, loosening, and mechanical failure. Alternative strategies aimed at restoring pelvic continuity and achieving biological fixation may improve construct stability and clinical outcomes.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 19 patients with intraoperatively confirmed pelvic discontinuity who underwent revision total hip arthroplasty between 2014 and 2024. Patients were divided into three groups according to the reconstruction technique used: Group 1 (n = 8) underwent anti-protrusio cage reconstruction alone, Group 2 (n = 6) received additional anterior quadrilateral surface plating prior to cage implantation, and Group 3 (n = 5) underwent restoration of pelvic continuity through anterior and posterior column fixation followed by implantation of a porous-coated primary acetabular cup. Clinical and radiological outcomes were assessed with a minimum follow-up of 2 years, including complications, loosening, reoperation, and reoperation-free survival.

RESULTS: Nineteen patients (mean age 71.2 years) with intraoperatively confirmed pelvic discontinuity were included. Aseptic loosening rates differed significantly among the three groups (P = 0.039), occurring in 50% of patients in Group 1 and in none of the patients in Groups 2 or 3. Reoperation rates were higher in Group 1 (75%) than in Group 2 (16.7%) and Group 3 (20%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.074). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated a trend toward lower reoperation-free survival in Group 1; however, differences among the groups were not statistically significant (log-rank P = 0.237).

CONCLUSION: Reconstruction strategies involving restoration of pelvic continuity through column stabilization may provide improved mechanical stability and lower complication rates compared with conventional cage-only techniques in the management of pelvic discontinuity. In selected patients, bicolumnar fixation followed by implantation of a porous-coated primary acetabular cup may offer the additional advantage of biological fixation. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Arthroplasty centers logistically separated from general orthopedic departments were associated with a more successful implementation of a standardized day-case setup : A Danish cohort study of 6718 procedures from a fast-track multi-center collaboration.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Day-case hip and knee arthroplasty can reduce bed occupancy and improve cost-effectiveness, which is crucial for addressing the increasing demand among hip and knee osteoarthritis patients. This study investigated how different arthroplasty center setups were associated with the implementation and day-of-surgery (DOS) discharge rates of a standardized day-case setup.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We included unilateral primary hip and knee arthroplasty patients from seven fast-track arthroplasty centers, all implementing a standardized day-case setup in September 2022 with identical eligibility and discharge criteria. Centers were categorized as: Satellite Arthroplasty Centers (SACs): Only primary arthroplasties, separate logistics. Elective Arthroplasty Centers (EACs): Complex primaries, revisions, separate logistics. Arthroplasty Unit Orthopedic Departments (AUOs): Primary and revision procedures, integrated into a general orthopedic department. We compared DOS discharge rates from September 2022 to September 2023 with a baseline period (July 2019-December 2019) using crude percentages. We compared the DOS discharge rate for day-case-eligible patients in study period between the center types using mixed effects models.

RESULTS: We included 6718 patients (1357 SAC, 4309 EAC, 1052 AUO) during the study period and 3974 in the baseline period. DOS discharge rates increased post-implementation across all centers (SAC: 3.9% to 30%, EAC: 5.5% to 23%, AUO: 7.4% to 14%). Compared with AUOs (36%), successful DOS discharge among eligible patients was more likely in SACs (54%; adjusted OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.3-7.1; adjusted risk difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 5.9-44) and EACs (60%; adjusted OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.7-8.5; adjusted risk difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 13.8-48).

CONCLUSIONS: Arthroplasty centers with logistics separate from the general orthopedic department, SACs and EACs, were associated with higher rates of successful DOS discharge among eligible patients during implementation of a standardized day-case pathway, despite integrated arthroplasty units, AUOs, having higher day-case surgery use before implementation.

articles.title: Preoperative coronal tibiofemoral subluxation does not affect 2-year outcomes after mobile-bearing medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty for anteromedial osteoarthritis.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Coronal tibiofemoral subluxation (CTFS) is frequently observed in patients with medial knee osteoarthritis; however, its clinical relevance and the acceptable degree of CTFS when considering unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) remain unclear. This study aimed to determine whether preoperative CTFS influences short-term postoperative clinical outcomes in patients with anteromedial osteoarthritis (AMOA) undergoing medial UKA.

METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 457 consecutive knees with AMOA who underwent mobile-bearing UKA performed at a single center between August 2016 and May 2023 were analyzed. CTFS, defined as medial translation of the femur relative to the tibia, was measured on preoperative weight-bearing anteroposterior radiographs and expressed as the percentage of tibial plateau width. Patients were categorized into mild (0-5%), moderate (≥ 5% to < 10%), and severe (≥ 10%) CTFS groups. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) preoperatively and at 3 months, 1 and 2 years postoperatively. Pairwise comparisons of changes in OKS were performed using a general linear model with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc tests, and adjusted mean differences were calculated controlling for age, sex, body mass index, and preoperative OKS.

RESULTS: At 2 years, mean OKS improvements were 16.6 ± 8.9, 14.8 ± 8.3, and 16.0 ± 9.3 in the mild, moderate, and severe CTFS groups, respectively. Adjusted mean differences between groups were small, with confidence intervals including zero. The severe CTFS group demonstrated greater joint line convergence angle than the mild and moderate groups (both p < 0.001). Mean bearing thickness did not differ among groups (p = 0.428).

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative CTFS was not associated with worse outcomes in mobile-bearing UKA for AMOA with correctable deformity. Within the setting of correctable deformity and appropriate patient selection, preoperative CTFS was not associated with inferior 2-year outcomes. Longer-term survivorship and radiographic progression analyses are warranted.

articles.title: Radial head arthroplasty restores axial construct stiffness in a Monteggia-like injury model: a biomechanical study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Monteggia-like lesions are rare but complex elbow injuries involving fractures of both the proximal ulna and the radial head. While the influence of ulnar alignment and soft tissue integrity on radial head stability has been extensively studied, the effect of radial head integrity on the stability of ulnar fixation remains poorly understood. Given the high rates of nonunion and revision surgery after proximal ulna fractures, improved understanding of forearm biomechanics in these combined injuries is highly clinically relevant as it influences the surgical strategy in primary care of these injuries. Accordingly, this study aimed to evaluate the biomechanical impact of radial head resection and radial head arthroplasty on forearm stiffness in a simulated Monteggia-like injury model. We hypothesized that radial head resection would reduce construct stiffness compared with both the native state and radial head arthroplasty, and that arthroplasty would partially restore stiffness toward native levels MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen human cadaveric elbow specimens were biomechanically tested under axial loading. After baseline testing in the native state, a standardized segmental comminution model was created and stabilized using locking plate osteosynthesis. Sequential testing was then performed after radial head resection and after implantation of a modular radial head prosthesis. Specimens were loaded cyclically up to 450 N for 1,000 cycles with the elbow positioned at 30° of flexion. Construct stiffness was calculated and compared between testing conditions.

RESULTS: Mean construct stiffness in the native state was 49.3 ± 4.29 N/mm and decreased significantly after creation and fixation of the ulnar defect (36.05 ± 6.71 N/mm). Radial head resection resulted in a further significant reduction in stiffness (25.83 ± 6.65 N/mm). Following radial head arthroplasty, stiffness increased to 33.8 ± 7.89 N/mm, representing a significant improvement compared with the resection state (p ≤ 0.0026). No significant difference was observed between stiffness after prosthesis implantation and the condition with intact radial head and stabilized ulna.

CONCLUSION: Radial head integrity significantly contributes to forearm stiffness in Monteggia-like lesions. Radial head arthroplasty partially restores biomechanical stability after resection and may alter load distribution in a manner that could be relevant for fixation durability. These findings support the need to address the radial column to optimize stability in complex elbow injuries.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Biomechanical study.

articles.title: Correction: Single double-loaded anchor repair of isolated Lafosse III subscapularis tears in patients not involved in physically demanding activities provides satisfactory functional and radiologic outcomes at minimum 5-year follow-up.
Comparison of surgically treated floating elbow injuries and supracondylar humeral fractures in children.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Floating elbow is a rare injury type in pediatric fractures. This study compared the differences in injury mechanisms, treatment modalities, complications and prognosis between floating elbow injury and supracondylar humerus fractures (SHF) in children in a surgically treated cohort.

METHODS: The retrospective analysis included patients with floating elbow and SHF treated at our hospital between May 2016 and May 2023. Sex, age, body mass index (BMI), mechanism of injury, affected limb, fracture displacement, presence of neurovascularinjury, type of injury, Gartland classification, and acute compartment syndrome (ACS) were analyzed. Elbow function was evaluated using the Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS). ACS was defined by clinical criteria including pain, paresthesia, and/or compartment pressure > 30 mmHg.

RESULTS: A total of 113 children were enrolled, including 27 in the floating elbow group (22 males, 5 females, median age 8 years [IQR 6-11 years]), and 86 in the SHF group (58 males, 28 females, median age 8 years [IQR 5-10 years]). Mechanism of injury (p = 0.001), fracture type (p = 0.003), and preoperative nerve injury (p = 0.001) differed significantly between the two groups. ACS incidence differed significantly between open and closed fractures in the floating elbow group (p = 0.028); however, this finding is based on a small number of events.

CONCLUSION: In this surgically treated cohort, we did not detect statistically significant differences in elbow function outcomes between children with floating elbow and those with isolated SHF. Open fractures were associated with a higher incidence of ACS in the floating elbow group compared with closed fractures, although the number of events was small (p = 0.028). Larger studies are needed to confirm equivalence or identify clinically meaningful differences.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

articles.title: Platelet-rich plasma for knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of structural outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To assess the impact of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) on imaging-based structural outcomes in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA).

METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to May 2026 evaluating imaging-based structural effects of PRP in knee OA. Risk ratio (RR) was used to evaluate binary outcomes and standardized mean differences (SMDs) or mean differences (MDs) for continuous endpoints, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

RESULTS: A total of 12 RCTs involving 1,200 patients were included. PRP was associated with greater improvement in patellofemoral cartilage thickness/volume compared with control treatments (SMD 0.94; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.34), whereas no significant differences were observed for medial tibial cartilage thickness/volume or cartilage defect progression. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based structural scores showed no between-group differences in Whole-Organ Magnetic Resonance Imaging Score (WORMS) osteophytes or subchondral cysts, although PRP demonstrated a significant reduction in bone marrow edema (SMD - 0.40; 95% CI, - 0.71 to - 0.09). Synovitis did not differ overall between groups (SMD - 0.22; 95% CI, - 0.43 to 0.00).

CONCLUSION: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, PRP demonstrated limited and inconsistent effects on imaging-based structural outcomes in knee OA, and did not confer significant and consistent benefits in medial tibial cartilage measurements, cartilage defect progression, synovitis, or most WORMS domains. The favorable findings observed for patellofemoral cartilage and bone marrow edema should be interpreted with caution. Thus, the findings do not provide clear evidence supporting PRP as a structural disease-modifying treatment, and additional high-quality RCTs using standardized imaging endpoints are warranted.

articles.title: First-in-human prospective pilot study of a bipolar dual-center total wrist arthroplasty: early mechanical stability and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Total wrist arthroplasty (TWA) is limited by implant loosening, instability, and non-physiological load transfer, partly because most contemporary implants rely on a single center of rotation and do not preserve native wrist kinematics. This first-in-human pilot study evaluated the feasibility, early mechanical stability, and clinical outcomes of a novel bipolar dual-center TWA system designed to preserve radiocarpal and midcarpal motion.

METHODS: This prospective single-center pilot case series included five consecutive patients with end-stage wrist arthritis treated with a bipolar dual-center TWA implant using cement fixation, as per the device's intended use. The outcome measures included pain assessed using the pain subscale of the Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) questionnaire (normalized to a 0-10 scale), total PRWE score, DASH score, range of motion, grip strength, radiographic implant stability, complications, and reoperation. Clinical outcomes were assessed at the most recent follow-up visit.

RESULTS: The mean follow-up was 19.2 months (range, 12-24 months), with 24-month data available for three patients. Implant survivorship was 100%, with no loosening, migration, dislocation, or implant revision observed on radiographs. One patient experienced a traumatic postoperative fall without loss of implant fixation. The mean PRWE-derived pain score improved from 9.0 to 3.0, and the mean PRWE total improved from 84.6 to 23.2 at the final follow-up. The mean DASH score improved from 79.0 to 29.5, with substantial inter-patient variability (final range, 0-91.7). All five patients met the predefined responder criterion of ΔPRWE ≥ 20 combined with radiographic stability. Three patients with positive preoperative signs of carpal tunnel syndrome subsequently underwent carpal tunnel release 4-8 months postoperatively, with symptomatic improvement in all patients. One intraoperative carpal fracture was managed without component revision surgery. The mean wrist flexion improved from 13° to 37°, and extension improved from 11° to 32°.

CONCLUSIONS: This first-in-human pilot study demonstrated the technical feasibility and early mechanical stability of the bipolar dual-center TWA concept. All patients met the predefined wrist-specific responder criteria with stable mechanical implant fixation. These findings support further investigation of the dual-center concept in larger studies with longer follow-up periods.

articles.title: The reliability and validity of the 30-Second Fast-Paced Walk Test in patients with total knee arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Walking speed is a significant measure of functional ability and recovery after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The 30-Second Fast-Paced Walk Test (30SFW) is a simple, low-cost, and easy-to-administer assessment method that evaluates short-distance walking ability.

OBJECTIVE: To investigate the reliability and validity of the 30SFW test in patients with TKA.

METHODS: This study was designed as a repeated-measures study conducted by one assessor. 38 patients with TKA who had undergone primary TKA at least 6 months earlier (mean age 70.11 ± 10.19 years) were included in the study. The 30SFW, the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) Knee Score, and Short Form (SF)-12 Quality of Life Questionnaire were administered to the patients. The 30SFW was administered twice at a single center on the same day, with an hour-long rest interval between sessions.

RESULTS: The test-retest reliability of the 30SFW was excellent. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC [2, 1]), minimal detectable change (MDC95), and standard error of the measurement (SEM) values were 0.98, 2.91, and 1.05, respectively, at the 95% confidence level. The Pearson correlation coefficient of the 30SFW with the physical component of the SF-12 was 0.45 (p = 0.005).

CONCLUSION: The 30SFW has excellent test-retest reliability and moderate concurrent validity in assessing walking ability in patients with TKA. The MDC95 was 2.91 m, indicating the minimum change required to exceed measurement error under similar testing conditions. Further studies are needed to determine the clinically important change and responsiveness of the 30SFW in this population.

articles.title: Net present value analysis of total salary compensation in hand surgery: academic versus non-academic careers.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Studies comparing salary compensation of hand surgeons in different practice settings have been limited. This study compared projected lifetime salary compensation between academic and non-academic hand surgeons.

METHODS: Compensation data were sourced from the 2025 Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) and American Medical Group Association (AMGA) salary benchmarks. Net present values of theoretical career paths in hand surgery were calculated assuming a 32-year career and a 3% discount rate. Sensitivity analyses were performed with variable discount rates and career lengths. Monte Carlo simulations were performed.

RESULTS: Academic practice demonstrated lower lifetime salary compensation than non-academic practice across career trajectories, sensitivity analyses, and Monte Carlo simulations using MGMA data with minimal differences using AMGA data. With MGMA, academic practice ($12.6 million) resulted in 19.7% lower lifetime salary compensation than non-academic practice ($15.7 million). With AMGA, academic practice ($15.0 million) resulted in 2.7% higher lifetime salary compensation than non-academic practice ($14.6 million). Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated lower lifetime salary compensation for academic practice with MGMA ($12.9 million versus $16.0 million, 19.4% difference, P < 0.001) but comparable compensation with AMGA data ($15.1 million versus $15.0 million, 0.7% difference, P = 0.182).

CONCLUSION: Hand surgeons in academic practice demonstrated lower lifetime salary compensation than their non-academic counterparts using MGMA data and similar compensation using AMGA data. While compensation alone does not fully capture the complexity of career decision making, this study may be useful to future hand surgeons and service line leaders.

articles.title: Complicated labral injuries in female patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip are associated with localized stress concentration in the superior acetabulum.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) alters joint mechanics and increases the risk of labral injury, compromising hip stability and leading to abnormal stress distribution and cartilage degeneration. However, the relationship between labral injury severity and joint loading stress in DDH remains unclear. This study investigated the effect of labral injury severity on stress distribution in DDH patients using computed tomography osteoabsorptometry (CT-OAM) and finite element analysis.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed 54 hips from 45 female patients undergoing joint-preserving surgery for DDH. Labral injuries were classified as simple or complicated on radial MRI. Subchondral bone density distribution was evaluated with CT-OAM, while finite element analysis of pelvic and femoral bones with cartilage was performed under a single-leg stance to assess contact pressure and area. Statistical analyses examined associations between labral injury severity and stress distribution.

RESULTS: Superior injuries showed significantly increased high-density area (HDA) in the superior acetabulum, indicating localized stress concentration (simple injury vs. complicated injury, 64.4% vs. 80.3%, p < 0.001). However, finite element analysis revealed no significant differences in contact pressure or area (simple vs. complicated, 5.3 N/mm² vs. 6.2 N/mm², p = 0.538), which we interpret as showing that bony morphology alone could not explain the observed stress patterns. Instead, the discrepancy highlights the role of labral failure reflected in CT-derived subchondral bone density.

CONCLUSION: Complicated labral injuries, especially superiorly, were associated with localized stress accumulation in DDH.

articles.title: Postoperative alignment and patients reported outcome measures improvement after high tibial osteotomy: a significant interaction with osteoarthritis severity.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Optimal postoperative alignment in high tibial osteotomy (HTO) remains controversial due to inconsistent target definitions and limited evidence supporting osteoarthritis (OA) severity-based strategies. This study evaluated clinical outcomes across postoperative weight-bearing line (WBL) categories stratified by OA severity, hypothesizing that overcorrection would be detrimental in early OA but not in advanced OA.

METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 181 knees that underwent open-wedge or closed-wedge HTO between 2017 and 2023 with a minimum 2-year follow-up. Knees were classified as early OA (Kellgren-Lawrence [KL] ≤ 2) or advanced OA (KL ≥ 3). The corrective angle was defined as the planned angular change required to shift the mechanical axis to the target postoperative alignment, determined by aiming for a postoperative %WBL of 62.5% on double-limb standing full-length radiographs. Overcorrection was defined as %WBL ≥ 70%. Clinical and radiographic outcomes were assessed at baseline and final follow-up. Multivariable regression models identified factors associated with changes (Δ) in Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12) and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), and logistic regression evaluated achievement of minimum clinically important difference (MCID) and patient acceptable symptom state (PASS). Each knee was treated as an independent observational unit.

RESULTS: Early OA (n = 112) and advanced OA (n = 69) showed comparable baseline characteristics. In early OA, postoperative alignment was significantly associated with ΔFJS‑12 and ΔKOOS Sports. Compared with optimal alignment, overcorrection was associated with smaller improvement in ΔFJS‑12 (β = -10.49, 95% CI - 20.46 to - 0.53) and ΔKOOS Sports, whereas undercorrection did not demonstrate a statistically significant association with postoperative improvement. Overcorrection also reduced the likelihood of achieving MCID and PASS in early OA. In advanced OA, postoperative alignment was not associated with PROM improvements or MCID/PASS achievement.

CONCLUSIONS: Overcorrection was associated with significantly poorer improvement in FJS-12 and KOOS Sports in early OA, whereas postoperative alignment was not associated with differences in PROM improvements in advanced OA.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV.

articles.title: Analysis of serological markers and synovial fluid cytology in aseptic revision total knee arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Recent studies examining synovial fluid analysis to differentiate causes for aseptic revision total knee arthroplasty (rTKA) were limited to aseptic loosening and instability. This study aims to establish specific serological and synovial profiles for various rTKA etiologies.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent aseptic rTKA at a single academic institution between 2012 and 2023. Inclusion required complete serum inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)) and synovial fluid differentials within three months pre-operatively. Periprosthetic joint infections were strictly excluded utilizing the 2018 International Consensus Meeting criteria. In total, 156 patients were included and stratified into five aseptic etiologies: aseptic loosening (50.6%), instability (28.2%), arthrofibrosis (16.7%), liner wear (2.6%), and component malposition (1.9%). Serological markers were evaluated utilizing a multivariate general linear model adjusting for patient demographics, while synovial markers were assessed via Welch's Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Games-Howell post-hoc testing.

RESULTS: Multivariate analysis demonstrated that the underlying rTKA indication was not a significant independent predictor of elevated ESR (P = 0.661) or CRP (P = 0.947). Welch's ANOVA revealed significant differences in the percentage of synovial monocytes (P < 0.001) and lymphocytes (P = 0.010), alongside the polymorphonuclear cells/monocyte (P = 0.030) and lymphocyte/monocyte (P = 0.005) ratios. Games-Howell post-hoc testing demonstrated the tibial liner wear group exhibited significantly higher monocyte percentages, paired with lower lymphocyte percentages and cellular ratios, compared to other aseptic etiologies.

CONCLUSIONS: This study revealed that routine systemic inflammatory markers and standard synovial fluid cell counts do not significantly vary among the common etiologies of aseptic rTKA. Nonetheless, tibial polyethylene liner wear appears to elicit an exploratory, monocyte-predominant and lymphocyte-depleted local macrophage response that is absent in other mechanisms of aseptic failure. Further research with larger cohorts is warranted to validate this association and explore its potential as a diagnostic tool.

articles.title: Clinical outcomes and feasibility of a fast-track protocol after total ankle replacement: a prospective study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Postoperative recovery after total ankle replacement remains challenging, and evidence supporting the use of fast-track protocols in this setting is limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the short-term clinical outcomes and safety of a fast-track protocol following total ankle replacement.

METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted on consecutive adult patients undergoing primary total ankle replacement through an anterior approach between January 2023 and June 2024. All procedures were performed by a single experienced surgeon using the same implant. The fast-track protocol included early postoperative mobilization, multimodal pain management, bleeding control, and structured physiotherapy with standardized discharge criteria. Ankle function was assessed using the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society's (AOFAS) Ankle Hindfoot Scale preoperatively and at hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included time to active ankle mobilization, time to assisted ambulation with crutches, length of hospital stay, and wound healing evaluated using the ASEPSIS wound score.

RESULTS: Twenty-two patients were included. Median AOFAS Ankle Hindfoot Scale scores improved significantly from 29.0 preoperatively to 68.0 at discharge. Active ankle mobilization was achieved after a median of two days, assisted ambulation after three days, and the median hospital stay was five days. Wound healing outcomes were favourable, with low ASEPSIS scores and only one minor wound complication managed conservatively. No major wound complications, infections, or prosthesis-related adverse events were observed.

CONCLUSION: In this prospective single-arm study, a fast-track protocol following total ankle replacement was feasible and was associated with early functional recovery and favourable short-term safety outcomes. These findings should be interpreted as preliminary and descriptive, given the absence of a control group. Larger comparative studies with longer follow-up are needed to determine its effectiveness relative to conventional postoperative care.

articles.title: Patient-specific management in high-risk revision total hip arthroplasty: mid-term outcomes of a next-generation constrained acetabular liner.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Managing recurrent instability in revision total hip arthroplasty (rTHA) requires a personalized approach, as traditional constrained liners often yield suboptimal results due to locking-mechanism failure and limited impingement-free range of motion. This study aimed to evaluate the mid-term clinical outcomes of a novel constrained acetabular liner (CAL) when utilized as a patient-specific solution for a high-risk cohort undergoing complex rTHA. By tailoring the constraint to individual biomechanical deficits, this next-generation device seeks to mitigate historic failure modes.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 32 patients who underwent 37 rTHA procedures with a next-generation CAL at a single urban academic center between March 2017 and October 2023. Average follow-up was 4.7 years (range, 0.3 to 9.7 years). The most common indication for rTHA was instability (70.3%), followed by infection (16.2%), aseptic loosening (10.8%), and polyethylene wear (2.7%). Just over one third of patients (37.5%) had undergone a prior revision. Preoperative constructs included fixed-bearing (37.8%), dual-mobility (32.4%), CAL (24.3%), static spacer (2.7%), and hemiarthroplasty (2.7%).

RESULTS: In most procedures (70.3%), the CAL was implanted into a pre-existing acetabular cup, whereas 29.7% involved both cup and liner revision. Following rTHA, no cases of implant wear, breakage, acetabular cup aseptic loosening, or periprosthetic fracture were observed. Six patients (18.8%) underwent a total of sixteen subsequent reoperations after CAL implantation-10 for instability and 6 for infection. Among instability-related reoperations, 4 involved revision to a new next-generation CAL. Survivorship free from all-cause reoperation was 83.8% at one year and 72.6% at latest follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates favorable mid-term clinical outcomes and reoperation-free survivorship following complex revision THA using a novel constrained acetabular liner system. For patient cohorts suffering from severe recurrent dislocation, this next-generation CAL provides an effective, tailored tool in the surgical armamentarium by adapting to unique patient anatomy and soft-tissue compromises. Further research with larger sample sizes and extended follow-up is needed to assess long-term durability.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of standard practice wrist MRI for scapholunate ligament injuries: a retrospective arthroscopic correlation study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The scapholunate ligament is the most injured intercarpal ligament. Untreated tears can lead to carpal instability and subsequent radiocarpal and midcarpal osteoarthritis. While wrist arthroscopy remains the gold standard, the diagnostic performance of standard practice preoperative MRI in clinical practice warrants further investigation.

METHODS: We retrospectively analysed patients who underwent preoperative wrist MRI followed by wrist arthroscopy between 2013 and 2021. MRI findings regarding scapholunate ligament integrity were compared with arthroscopic findings serving as reference standard. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated for detection of any scapholunate ligament lesion (partial or complete tear).

RESULTS: A total of 889 patients were included. Complete paired data were available for 864 patients with a mean age of 42.4 ± 15.4 years (range 10-83 years). 51.3% were male. MRI classified the ligament as intact in 83.9%, partially ruptured in 9.1%, and completely ruptured in 6.9%. Arthroscopy identified intact ligaments in 78.2%, partial tears in 12.9%, and complete tears in 8.9%. In this cohort, MRI demonstrated high specificity (91.1%, 95% CI 89.0-93.3) but limited sensitivity (42.0%, 95% CI 35.0-49.1) for scapholunate ligament lesions.

CONCLUSION: In standard clinical practice, preoperative wrist MRI shows high specificity but insufficient sensitivity for detecting scapholunate ligament injuries. In this cohort, MRI detected intact ligaments reliably, but a relevant proportion of partial and complete tears remained unrecognized.

articles.title: Correction: Robotic-arm assistance in revision total hip arthroplasty improves the accuracy of acetabular component positioning: a cadaver-based study.
Expert evaluation of ChatGPT-generated responses to patient questions in conventional and fast-track total knee arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fast-track total knee arthroplasty (TKA) asks patients to understand early mobilization, early discharge, opioid-sparing analgesia, and selective use of drains and catheters. We evaluated expert-rated quality of ChatGPT responses to patient questions about these pathway-specific concepts alongside conventional TKA questions.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this cross-sectional evaluation, three arthroplasty surgeons independently scored responses to 50 conventional TKA and 20 investigator-developed fast-track questions in four domains on 5-point scales. The conventional questions were selected by a multidisciplinary panel; the fast-track questions did not undergo the same selection process. Response-level means were compared descriptively and with exploratory Mann-Whitney U tests.

RESULTS: Seventy responses received 210 expert assessments. Recalculated mean ± SD scores across individual ratings were 4.99 ± 0.15 for accuracy, 4.98 ± 0.14 for completeness, 4.98 ± 0.17 for safety, and 5.00 ± 0.07 for readability. Each of the 20 fast-track responses received a score of 5 from each of the three raters in all four domains (Supplementary Table S1). Nevertheless, question-set construction differed and scores clustered at the ceiling, so the exploratory comparison does not establish equivalence.

CONCLUSIONS: Experts gave high ratings to the evaluated responses, including those on fast-track concepts. The observed data do not establish equivalence between question sets: the fast-track ratings require source-data verification, the sets were selected differently, and scores were concentrated at the maximum. Clinician review remains appropriate for protocol-dependent and safety-related advice.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

articles.title: Epidemiology, determinants, and microbiological profile of implant-associated infections following intramedullary nailing in a tertiary hospital in Ethiopia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Implant-associated infections after intramedullary nailing (IMN) are a major cause of morbidity in patients with long bone fractures. This study aimed to determine the magnitude, determinants, and microbiological profile of such infections in a tertiary hospital in Ethiopia.

METHODS: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 260 patients who underwent IMN for lower extremity long bone fractures between January 2021 and December 2023. Clinical data, operative details, and microbiological results were collected, and logistic regression was applied to identify determinants of infection.

RESULTS: The overall infection rate was 8.46% (95% CI: 5.38-12.53; 22/260), comprising 4.62% deep and 3.85% superficial infections. We found that emergency surgery and hospital stay longer than 14 days were independently associated with an increased risk of infection. Among the limited number of culture-positive infections, Gram-negative bacteria predominated, with Escherichia coli as the most frequently identified pathogen.

CONCLUSION: The infection rate was higher than in many other settings, underscoring the need for improved perioperative infection prevention and reduced hospital stays. Findings highlight the importance of perioperative optimization and hospital infection control in LMICs.

articles.title: Notch-referenced mediolateral verification of tibial tunnel position in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a 3D imaging validation study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Non-anatomic tibial tunnel placement remains a leading contributor to anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) failure. Mediolateral (ML) tunnel positioning is particularly difficult intraoperatively because no consistent bony landmark defines the lateral footprint border.

PURPOSE: To evaluate the accuracy of a novel intraoperative Notch-Referenced Mediolateral (NRML) verification technique by comparing the ML position of the tibial tunnel center (TTC) on postoperative 3D CT with the native tibial footprint center (TFC) on preoperative 3D MRI.

METHODS: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, 108 consecutive patients underwent primary all-inside single-bundle ACLR with intraoperative NRML verification. This arthroscopic technique uses the intercondylar notch as a visual reference to verify mediolateral tibial tunnel position before definitive drilling. TFC and TTC were independently measured on preoperative 3D MRI and postoperative 3D CT using a standardized quadrant-grid protocol by two blinded observers. The primary outcome was ML deviation (tunnel - footprint). MRI-CT agreement and measurement reliability were assessed with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis.

RESULTS: The anatomical TFC was located at 46.1 ± 2.3% of tibial plateau width in the ML direction, versus 44.8 ± 2.0% for the TTC. Mean ML deviation was -1.01 ± 1.52 mm (p < 0.001), a small but statistically significant medial bias; 91.7% (95% CI 84.9-95.6%) of tunnels fell within ±3 mm of the native footprint. MRI-CT agreement was good (ICC 0.81-0.85), and inter/intraobserver reliability was good to excellent (ICC 0.78-0.89). No significant associations were found between ML deviation and sex, injury chronicity, graft diameter, or plateau size.

CONCLUSION: In this single-arm cohort,NRML verification is a simple, equipment-free technique that placed the tibial tunnel within ~1 mm of the native ML footprint, with high measurement reliability. Prospective comparative and outcome studies are needed to confirm its clinical value.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV.

articles.title: Preoperative pain and achievement of the minimal clinically important difference for physical function one year after total hip arthroplasty: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To examine the association between preoperative social, clinical, and biological variables and the achievement of the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) on the WOMAC-function subscale one year post total hip arthroplasty (THA).

METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 85 patients (aged ≥ 65) completed baseline preoperative assessment, and 53 completed the 12-month follow-up (32 lost to follow-up; 66.0% achieved MCID). The outcome was achieving WOMAC-function MCID (≥ 26.54 points). Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for baseline pain, age, sex, and BMI were performed. ROC curves evaluated discriminative capacity.

RESULTS: An exploratory ROC analysis identified a baseline pain threshold of 6.5 on the Numerical Rating Scale yielded an AUC of 0.740 (70% sensitivity, 77% specificity).

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative pain intensity independently associated with clinically meaningful functional improvement post-THA. An exploratory pain threshold of 6.5 on the NRS may provide an exploratory benchmark for future risk stratification.

articles.title: The boundary between microbial detection and implant-related infection: a structured narrative review of analytical credibility, biological persistence, host response, and clinical causality.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Unexpected microbial signals are frequently encountered in patients with orthopaedic implants who do not satisfy validated criteria for confirmed infection. The central interpretive problem is not limited to periprosthetic joint infection (PJI); it also arises in fracture-fixation and spinal instrumentation, and it involves conventional culture, sonication, histopathology, broad-range polymerase chain reaction (PCR), 16 S rRNA sequencing, and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS).

METHODS: We performed a structured narrative review of literature identified in PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science, updated through 27 June 2026. Eligible publications addressed microbial or biofilm-associated signals in orthopaedic implants without unequivocal infection at the time of sampling, or reported outcomes after unexpected positive cultures. Evidence was organized by implant type, indication for implant removal, detection method, host-response evidence, and longitudinal outcome. Particular attention was paid to the distinction between routinely removed fracture-fixation devices and failure-related arthroplasty or spinal revisions.

RESULTS: Routine removal of fracture-fixation devices provides the least confounded clinical window and demonstrates that microbial signals may be recovered from implants in the absence of recognized failure or overt infection. By contrast, arthroplasty and spinal cohorts labelled "presumed aseptic" are intrinsically confounded because pain, loosening, osteolysis, or pseudarthrosis may represent occult infection. Molecular positivity is further limited by low-biomass contamination and inability to distinguish viable organisms from relic DNA. Favorable outcomes after revision do not prove that infection was never present, because revision surgery itself may eradicate or substantially reduce an occult microbial burden.

CONCLUSIONS: Microbial detection should be interpreted through three sequential domains: analytical credibility, biological activity or persistence, and clinical causality supported by host response or implant-related pathology. "Stable coexistence" is best treated as a longitudinal clinical phenotype or testable mechanistic hypothesis, not as an established diagnostic category. This framework complements, but does not replace, validated PJI, fracture-related infection (FRI), or other implant-specific definitions.

articles.title: Fewer poor joint awareness results with cementless TKA compared with the same-design cemented implant.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Comparisons of cemented and cementless TKA have focused on mean outcomes and generally reported equivalence. We hypothesized that a 3D-printed full-titanium cementless TKA and the same-design cemented implant would not differ significantly in average joint awareness but would differ in the proportion of patients with the poorest results, and we compared the two both at the mean and across the outcome distribution.

METHODS: Prospective two-cohort study of 109 primary unilateral TKAs (54 cementless, 55 cemented) for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, with complete 24-month follow-up. Exclusion criteria were valgus deformity and bilateral surgery. The primary outcome was the FJS-12, analysed both at the mean (multivariable linear regression, with propensity score overlap weighting as sensitivity analysis) and across its distribution (quantile regression). Secondary outcomes were PASS achievement (FJS-12 ≥ 33.3), OKS, and time to functional satisfaction.

RESULTS: The cementless group was younger (P < 0.001) with more men (P = 0.008). Mean FJS-12 was not different between groups after adjustment (β = 7.4, 95% CI - 1.8 to 16.6, P = 0.115), although the confidence interval did not exclude a difference exceeding the minimal clinically important difference; this finding was reproduced by overlap weighting. On quantile regression, cementless patients scored significantly higher at the 10th and 25th percentiles (adjusted P = 0.028 and 0.021) but not at the median or above. A greater proportion of cementless patients achieved the PASS (96.3% vs. 76.4%; absolute difference 19.9%, 95% CI 7.1 to 32.9; number needed to treat 5), which persisted after adjustment (P = 0.005). No significant differences were observed in OKS (P = 0.91) or time to functional satisfaction (adjusted P = 0.39). No revisions or loosening occurred.

CONCLUSION: The 3D-printed full-titanium cementless TKA did not produce a significantly higher mean FJS-12 than the same-design cemented device at 24 months, but it significantly reduced the proportion of patients with poor joint awareness outcomes.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

articles.title: Elective primary total hip arthroplasty in rheumatoid arthritis versus osteoarthritis: in-hospital outcomes from the national inpatient sample, 2016-2021.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether coded rheumatoid arthritis (RA) among patients undergoing elective total hip arthroplasty (THA) is associated with excess short-term inpatient morbidity in contemporary U.S. practice remains uncertain.

METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2021). Adults undergoing elective primary THA were identified using ICD-10-CM/PCS codes. The exposure cohort included admissions with coded RA in any diagnosis position. The comparator cohort included admissions with narrow primary hip osteoarthritis (OA) as the principal diagnosis and no RA. Propensity scores were estimated from demographic, socioeconomic, hospital, and comorbidity variables. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survey weighting was used for the primary analysis, followed by doubly adjusted regression models that included age and all variables with persistent post-weighting imbalance greater than 0.10 (female sex, osteoporosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic anemia, depression, and race). Additional sensitivity analyses included stricter weight truncation, a restriction analysis, conventional multivariable modeling, and sex-stratified analyses addressing residual sex imbalance.

RESULTS: A total of 274,582 admissions met eligibility criteria; 274,539 were included in the final analytic cohort after exclusion of 43 records with missing or invalid propensity-weight inputs. The analytic cohort included 7,264 RA admissions and 267,275 OA admissions. In the primary weighted analysis, RA was associated with higher odds of acute blood loss anemia (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.23-1.38), red blood cell transfusion (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.23-1.60), acute kidney injury (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.26-1.71), non-home discharge (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.19-1.36), and a composite hematologic/renal in-hospital complication (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.24-1.39).RA was also associated with slightly longer length of stay (+ 0.14 days, 95% CI + 0.10 to + 0.19) and modestly higher total hospital charges (+$1,018, 95% CI +$89 to +$1,947). Findings were directionally consistent across sensitivity analyses, including stricter weight truncation, restriction to admissions with principal OA plus concomitant RA, and sex-stratified analyses.

CONCLUSIONS: In this contemporary national THA cohort, coded RA was associated with a small but consistent increase in in-hospital complication and resource-utilization burden compared with OA. These findings should be interpreted as adjusted associations rather than causal effects, and the modest effect sizes should not be overstated. They may provide context for perioperative risk assessment and discharge planning among patients with coded RA undergoing elective THA.

articles.title: Research trends in total knee arthroplasty in India: a five-year bibliometric analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA) is one of the fastest-growing orthopaedic procedures in India, driven by demographic transitions, increased life expectancy, and the rising burden of knee osteoarthritis. With expanding procedural volumes, periodic evaluation of scientific output is essential to identify evolving research priorities, institutional leadership, and collaborative patterns. This study aimed to perform a bibliometric analysis of Indian TKA research published over the past five years.

METHODS: Publications were retrieved from the Scopus database using a structured search strategy for TKA-related terms. The search was restricted to studies published between 1 January 2021 and 30 December 2025 and conducted in an Indian setting. Bibliometric indicators assessed publication trends, document types, journals, authorship, institutional productivity, and state-wise contributions. Network-based bibliometric visualizations were generated using VOSviewer.

RESULTS: A total of 860 publications were identified, showing a steady increase in research output with peak productivity in 2025 (n = 221). Maharashtra and Delhi were the leading contributors, and the All-India Institute of Medical Sciences was the most productive institution. Original research articles accounted for 69.5% of publications. Emerging themes included robotic-assisted surgery, AI-based modeling, and advanced rehabilitation. International collaboration was observed in 24.18% of studies, mainly with the UK and USA.

CONCLUSION: Indian TKA research has demonstrated substantial growth and increasing thematic maturity over the past five years, with a shift toward technology-driven and collaborative research. Strengthening national registries, encouraging multicentric collaboration, and expanding research beyond metropolitan centers are essential to sustain future impact.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

articles.title: Round versus tape sutures with interference fit anchors perform similarly in cadaveric glenoid and greater tuberosity biomechanical testing.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine whether suture shape (flat-tape vs. round-wire) influences biomechanical performance at the suture-anchor-bone interface in interference-fit anchors used for rotator cuff and glenoid labrum repair.

METHODS: Four matched pairs of human cadaveric shoulders were used for the glenoid model, with six anchor sites per glenoid. Five matched pairs of cadaveric humeri were used for the rotator cuff model, with three anchor sites per humerus. Each model tested multiple suture-anchor constructs under cyclic loading followed by load-to-failure. Biomechanical outcomes included cyclic displacement, yield characteristics, ultimate failure strength, stiffness, and force at fixed displacements. A linear mixed-effects model was used to compare suture types, with suture type and anchor position as fixed effects and specimen as a random effect.

RESULTS: In the glenoid/labrum model, there were no significant differences among suture types in cyclic displacement (cycles 1, 50, or 100; p = 0.376, 0.101, 0.109), displacement at yield (p = 0.406), yield force (p = 0.880), force at 1 mm (p = 0.264) or 5 mm (p = 0.085), or ultimate failure strength (p = 0.204). Stiffness (p = 0.050) and force at 2 mm displacement (p = 0.033) differed at the overall model level, however, no significant pairwise differences were observed. In the humerus/rotator cuff model, displacement at cycle 50 (p = 0.022) and cycle 100 (p = 0.019) differed overall, although post hoc comparisons were not significant. Ultimate strength (p = 0.037), yield force (p = 0.012), and stiffness (p = 0.005) differed among groups, with post hoc analysis showing greater ultimate strength, yield force, and stiffness for 2-mm FiberTape compared with 2-mm XbraidTT. No other pairwise comparisons were significant.

CONCLUSION: Suture shape did not meaningfully influence interference-fit fixation properties in the glenoid and humeral models evaluated in this study. Tape-type and round-type sutures demonstrated comparable biomechanical performance at the suture-anchor interface within the tested constructs.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Controlled Laboratory Study.

articles.title: Association of systemic bone mineral density and tibial cortical thickness with postoperative subsidence after surgical treatment of tibial plateau fractures.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tibial plateau fractures are common fractures above the age of 50 years old and are frequently considered osteoporosis-associated fractures. However, the association between bone mineral density (BMD) and postoperative articular subsidence remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess whether there was an association between systemic BMD or tibial cortical thickness and articular subsidence after surgical treatment of tibial plateau fractures. Secondary objectives were to evaluate preoperative fracture displacement and the prevalence of reduced BMD in this cohort according to WHO criteria.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, patients treated surgically for low-energy tibial plateau fractures between 2017 and 2024 who underwent Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) within 12 months before or after injury were included. DEXA-derived T-scores were used to assess systemic bone density and Tibial Cortical Thickness (TCT) was used as a measure of tibial cortical bone status. Fracture subsidence and preoperative displacement were measured in the coronal plane using articular depression. Multivariable linear regression analyses were performed adjusting for age, BMI and fracture comminution. The primary outcome was also adjusted for preoperative articular depression.

RESULTS: Fifty-nine patients were included in the analysis. There were 57 women and 2 men. Mean age was 63.9 years (SD ± 8.1) and mean BMI was 26.2 (SD ± 4.8). Schatzker type II was the most common fracture pattern (30/59, 50.8%), followed by Schatzker type VI (20/59, 33.9%). According to WHO criteria, 1.7% had normal bone mineral density, 49.2% had osteopenia and 49.2% had osteoporosis. There was no statistically significant association between postoperative subsidence and systemic BMD (p = 0.259) or TCT (p = 0.340). Nor was there a statistically significant association between preoperative articular depression and systemic BMD (p = 0.132) or TCT (p = 0.397).

CONCLUSIONS: In this study, no statistically significant association was identified between systemic BMD or tibial cortical thickness and postoperative articular subsidence or preoperative depression, although the limited sample size warrants cautious interpretation. Osteoporosis and osteopenia were common in this selected cohort of DEXA-assessed patients above the age of 50 years with surgically treated low-energy tibial plateau fractures.

articles.title: Comorbidity burden and fracture pattern as predictors of early postoperative medical complications following bipolar hemiarthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Postoperative medical complications substantially affect outcomes after bipolar hemiarthroplasty (BHA) for displaced femoral neck fractures, with an impact comparable to surgical factors. This study aimed to identify risk factors for postoperative medical complications, focusing on comorbidities, polypharmacy, and fracture pattern.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 310 hips in 297 patients undergoing BHA. Baseline characteristics, comorbidities, and medication profiles were evaluated using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI), and comorbidity-polypharmacy score (CPS). The primary outcome was medical complications within 30 days. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors, and 1-year survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis.

RESULTS: Medical complications occurred in 53.7% of hips, most commonly delirium (17.0%). In the CCI-based model, age at surgery (odds ratio [OR] 1.05; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01-1.08; p = 0.006), displaced transcervical fractures (AO/OTA 31B2.1-31B2.2) (OR 2.07; 95% CI, 1.18-3.61; p = 0.011), displaced basicervical fractures (AO/OTA 31B2.3-31B3) (OR 4.67; 95% CI, 1.45-15.00; p = 0.010), a medium CCI category (OR 3.58; 95% CI, 1.10-11.60; p = 0.034), and a very high CCI category (OR 12.80; 95% CI 2.27-72.10; p = 0.004) were independently associated with complications. In the ECI-based model, age (OR 1.04; 95% CI, 1.01-1.07; p = 0.016), displaced transcervical fractures (OR 1.88; 95% CI 1.10-3.22; p = 0.021), and displaced basicervical fractures (OR 4.71; 95% CI 1.50-14.80; p = 0.008) remained significant predictors. One-year survival was 94.2% and was significantly lower among patients with higher CCI scores.

CONCLUSIONS: Comorbidity burden and fracture pattern are significant predictors of early postoperative medical complications after BHA for displaced femoral neck fractures. Incorporating these factors into preoperative risk stratification may facilitate optimized perioperative management and improve clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Hemi-hamate arthroplasties for proximal interphalangeal joint fracture dislocations: long-term follow-up in acute, subacute and chronic cases.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hemihamate arthroplasty (HHA) method is one of the recommended treatment methods for unstable proximal interphalangeal joint (PIPJ) fracture dislocations The primary goal of this method is to achieve a stable and well-aligned joint by reconstructing the palmar lip. The aim of this study is to present mid to long term results of patients treated with HHA method in the acute, subacute and chronically.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: 22 patients was operated with this technique by single surgeon between 2013 and 2025. Patients were classified as acute (< 3 weeks), subacute (3-6 weeks), and chronic (> 6 weeks) based on the time elapsed between the date of injury and the date of surgery. Patients were assessed clinically, radiologically and subjectively.

RESULTS: The mean ROM of the PIPJ was 80.6° (20-100°), the flexion was 91.6° (65-100), and the extension lag was 11° (0-50). Grip strength on the operated side was 91.7% of the average on the unaffected side (74-110). The mean rest pain score according to the VAS (0 least-10 most) was 0.6 (0-3), and the activity pain score was 2 (0-5). The mean Q-DASH scores assessing functional level were 9.55 and the mean Mayo scores were 81.4. When patients were asked about their satisfaction after surgery, 12 patients responded very good, two patients good, and four patients moderate.

CONCLUSIONS: With HHA, reasonable PIPJ ROM and good functional outcomes were achieved. With increased PIP ROM, functional outcomes statistically significantly improved. Thanks to hemihamate arthroplasty, successful results can be achieved even in cases where almost the entire joint surface is affected. Hemihamate arthroplasty method provides good functional results even in chronic injuries lasting up to a year, as in acute injuries.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV.

articles.title: Partial triceps tendon transfer for dynamic stabilization in posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow: a biomechanical study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) of the elbow results from lateral collateral ligament complex (LCLC) insufficiency. In the setting of failed conventional ligament reconstruction, no established salvage procedure is available. This study biomechanically evaluated partial triceps tendon transfer to the supinator crest as a dynamic stabilization concept for PLRI.

METHODS: Nine fresh-frozen human elbow specimens underwent cyclic external rotational loading of 0.5 Nm. Specimens were tested sequentially in the native state, an LCLC/common extensor origin-deficient unstable state, after transosseous LCLC repair, and after partial triceps tendon transfer to the supinator crest with the LCLC detached. Testing was performed under combined biceps/triceps loading conditions with external forearm rotation relative to the humerus as the primary outcome. A two-factor repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) compared unstable, repaired, and tendon-transfer conditions across loading conditions. The native state was assessed unloaded and reported separately in a one-factor RM-ANOVA.

RESULTS: Intervention significantly affected external rotation (F(2,16) = 33.31, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.81). Across loading conditions, partial triceps transfer significantly reduced external rotation compared to the unstable state (mean difference [MD]=-3.38°, p = 0.005), while LCLC repair showed lower external rotation than triceps tendon transfer (MD=-3.13°, p = 0.012). External rotation also differed significantly across the combined biceps/triceps loading conditions (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected F(1.26,10.11) = 77.00, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.91), decreasing from 13.37° at 0 kg biceps/0 kg triceps to 2.42° at 0.5 kg biceps/4.0 kg triceps.

CONCLUSION: Partial triceps tendon transfer improved dynamic elbow stabilization and significantly reduced PLRI in a LCLC‑deficient in vitro model. However, it did not fully restore joint stability, supporting its role as a potential adjunct or salvage option rather than a primary procedure. The findings highlight the importance of dynamic muscle tension in lateral elbow stability, while the time‑zero, in vitro design limits direct clinical translation and warrants further in vivo investigations.

articles.title: Development and validation of a model to predict full thickness rotator cuff tear.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Full-thickness rotator cuff tear (FTRCT) often requires surgical treatment. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the diagnostic gold standard; however, it is costly and resource-intensive. We aimed to develop and validate a clinical prediction model for FTRCT in patients with RCI, with the goal of identifying those at high risk at the initial visit.

METHODS: This prospective study consecutively enrolled patients clinically diagnosed with RCI from May 2025 to September 2025. All patients underwent shoulder MRI to confirm the presence or absence of FTRCT. Potential predictors involving demographic characteristics, clinical history, and physical examination findings, were collected. Predictor selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, followed by multivariable logistic regression to construct a risk prediction model, and then a nomogram was developed.

RESULTS: 357 patients were included, MRI confirmed FTRCT in 166 patients (46.5%). Patients were randomly divided into a training set (n = 249) and a test set (n = 108). LASSO regression identified 10 candidate predictors, and multivariable logistic regression identified physical labor, history of trauma, age, daily pain score, pain duration, and physical examination shoulder strength as independent predictors of FTRCT. The nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.910 (95% CI, 0.88-0.95), with 88% sensitivity, 82% specificity, and a C-index of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.83-0.95). Calibration and decision curve analyses supported its accuracy and clinical utility. CONCLUSIONS : This study developed a preliminary clinical nomogram for predicting FTRCT in patients with RCI, which showed good performance in internal validation and may help support early risk assessment and MRI triage. Its generalizability should be confirmed in external cohorts.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

articles.title: Minimally invasive circumferential fixation using TIFI and INFIX for unstable pelvic ring injuries: a prospective evaluation of clinical and radiological outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the clinical and radiological outcomes of minimally invasive circumferential fixation using combined trans-iliac internal fixation (TIFI) and anterior internal fixation (INFIX) in unstable pelvic ring injuries.

METHODS: A prospective study was conducted between 2022 and 2023 including 30 patients with unilateral unstable pelvic fractures (Tile B2 and C1). Patients were followed for a minimum of 12 months (mean 22 ± 4.7 months). Functional outcomes were assessed using the Majeed Score and Pelvic Outcome Score. Radiological assessment included displacement measurements, reduction quality, maintenance of reduction, and time to union.

RESULTS: Thirty patients (mean age 32.2 ± 14.9 years) were included. Mean operative time was 103.5 ± 10.5 min, blood loss 335 ± 65.8 mL, and fluoroscopy time 52 ± 14.7 s. Pelvic displacement improved from 15.8 ± 4.6 mm preoperatively to 3.6 ± 2.4 mm postoperatively, with a mean correction of 12.2 ± 4.5 mm and minimal loss of reduction (0.3 ± 0.8 mm). At one year, mean Majeed and Pelvic Outcome scores were 89.1 ± 5.6 and 34.6 ± 2.6, respectively. Mean time to union was 13.4 ± 2.1 weeks, with 90% excellent-good reductions (Matta criteria) and 100% union. Complications included superficial infection (13.3%), lateral femoral cutaneous nerve irritation (13.3%), and asymptomatic heterotopic ossification (3.3%).

CONCLUSION: Circumferential fixation using TIFI and INFIX achieved reliable reduction, maintained alignment until union, and was associated with favorable clinical and radiological outcomes in selected unstable pelvic ring injuries. The present findings demonstrate the feasibility and satisfactory performance of this technique; however, comparative studies are required to determine its relative advantages compared with other fixation strategies.

articles.title: Radiographic accuracy of implant positioning in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, does an imageless robotic system make a difference?
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robotic-assisted technologies and evolving implant designs have been introduced in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) to improve the accuracy and reproducibility of component positioning. However, the relative contribution of robotic assistance compared with conventional instrumentation to radiographic outcomes in experienced, high-volume centers remains unclear.

METHODS: This retrospective comparative study included 96 consecutive medial UKAs performed at a single high-volume institution. Patients were stratified into three groups: Journey I UKA implanted with NAVIO imageless robotic assistance (n = 38), Journey II Uni UKA implanted using conventional instrumentation (n = 27), and Journey II UK UKA implanted with CORI imageless robotic assistance (n = 31). Standardized standing long-leg weight-bearing radiographs were obtained preoperatively and postoperatively. Radiographic evaluation included hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle, femoral component coronal angle (FCCA), tibial component coronal angle (TCCA), and sagittal alignment parameters. Tibial coronal alignment was interpreted according to the Cartier metaphyseal alignment philosophy. Intergroup comparisons were performed using appropriate statistical tests.

RESULTS: Baseline demographic characteristics and preoperative radiographic parameters were comparable among the three groups (all p > 0.05). Postoperative mean HKA was 177.1° ± 2.1° in the Journey I NAVIO group, 177.3° ± 2.5° in the Journey II Uni conventional group, and 177.7° ± 2.2° in the Journey II UK CORI group, with no statistically significant differences (p = 0.56). Femoral and tibial component coronal alignment, including TCCA, showed no significant intergroup differences. All cases across the three cohorts were within predefined safe zones for HKA, FCCA, and TCCA. Sagittal alignment parameters were also comparable between groups.

CONCLUSION: In a high-volume center adopting a consistent alignment philosophy, medial UKA achieves equivalent and highly accurate radiographic outcomes regardless of robotic assistance or conventional instrumentation.

articles.title: The perforator-based axial adipofascial turnover flap combined with juncturae tendinum grafting for complex dorsal phalangeal defects.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Complex dorsal finger soft tissue defects remain a challenging reconstructive problem, particularly when associated with exposure of bone and extensor apparataus. Advances in the anatomical understanding of the dorsal cutaneous vascular system of the digits have allowed adipofascial flaps in this region to evolve from random-pattern to axial-pattern designs, improving vascular reliability. However, a structured and comprehensive approach for managing these combined defects has not been clearly defined in the literature. This study aims to present a holistic loco-regional strategy that optimizes the reconstructive ladder while minimizing donor-site morbidity and technical complexity.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This clinical series includes seven fingers with complex soft tissue defects involving the dorsal aspect of the middle and distal phalanges. All cases were managed using an ipsilateral loco-regional protocol consisting of three components: (1) an extended axial adipofascial turnover flap for soft tissue coverage, (2) tendon reconstruction using juncturae tendinum harvested from the fourth intermetacarpal space, and (3) full-thickness skin grafting from the wrist. Patients were followed for a minimum of six months. Functional outcomes were evaluated by range of motion and complication rates.

RESULTS: Complete flap survival was achieved in all cases. All fingers demonstrated satisfactory functional outcomes with acceptable flexion and extension ranges of motion at follow-up. No major complications, including infection, osteomyelitis, or significant donor-site morbidity, were observed.

CONCLUSIONS: The perforator-based axial adipofascial turnover flap combined with juncturae tendinum grafting provides reliable single-stage reconstruction of complex dorsal finger defects without the need for microsurgical anastomosis. This structured loco-regional approach enables immediate reconstruction without the need for microsurgical equipment or advanced microvascular expertise, offering a practical and reproducible alternative within the reconstructive ladder.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV.

articles.title: Operative treatment of high-grade medial collateral ligament injury and chronic medial knee instability: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: High-grade medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury and chronic medial knee instability can compromise both valgus and rotational control, especially in cruciate or multiligament injury. This systematic review evaluated operative treatment according to clinical phenotype rather than MCL grade alone. PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from January 1, 2000, to August 10, 2026; a Cochrane CENTRAL update was completed on September 7, 2026. Eligible clinical reports included operative treatment of acute high-grade MCL/medial-complex injury or chronic symptomatic medial instability. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, ROBINS-I, or the Joanna Briggs Institute case-series checklist. Thirty-five reports were included: 5 randomized or quasi-randomized trials, 9 nonrandomized comparative studies, and 21 case series. Routine acute medial surgery during ACL reconstruction was not consistently superior across heterogeneous grade III populations. In contrast, selected displaced distal or Stener-like lesions were plausible repair targets because interposition can prevent healing in apposition. Chronic symptomatic valgus and/or anteromedial rotatory insufficiency was most often treated with reconstruction, with directional improvement in objective stability and patient-reported outcomes in case series. Evidence for augmentation, the optimal reconstruction construct, and timing remains low certainty. Decisions should integrate repairability, residual valgus and rotational instability, associated ligament injury, alignment, and tissue quality. Prospective phenotype-stratified comparative studies using standardized stability, return-to-sport, complication, and long-term joint-preservation outcomes are required.Level of evidence: Level IV, systematic review of Level I-IV therapeutic studies.

articles.title: Correction: Recovery of gait after ankle fracture surgery following early mobilization and weight-bearing.
Factors associated with long-term patient-reported outcomes after periacetabular osteotomy.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Long-term survivorship and patient-reported outcomes after periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) have been reported; however, the relationships of long-term PROMs with preoperative cartilage degeneration and postoperative three-dimensional hip morphology remain incompletely understood. This study evaluated long-term PROMs and examined their associations with preoperative cartilage T2 values and postoperative hip morphology after PAO.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 42 hips in 42 patients with early-stage osteoarthritis who underwent PAO for developmental dysplasia of the hip and were followed for more than 10 years.
