BACKGROUND: While traditional surgical decision-making emphasizes long-term implant survivorship for octogenarians knee reconstruction, this paradigm may be inappropriate when patient mortality risk substantially exceeds revision risk. This study compared mid-term mortality between unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in octogenarians, hypothesizing that implant type would not significantly influence patient survival.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 238 consecutive octogenarian patients (age ≥ 80 years) who underwent primary knee arthroplasty at a single tertiary orthopaedic center between January 2018 and December 2020. Patients with revision arthroplasty, fracture, tumor, inflammatory arthropathy, or incomplete data were excluded. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at minimum 5-year follow-up. Secondary outcomes included age-stratified mortality (80-84, 85-89, ≥ 90 years) and identification of independent mortality predictors. Statistical analyses included independent t-tests, chi-square/Fisher's exact tests, standardized mean differences, and multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, follow-up duration, and registry year.

RESULTS: Of 238 patients, 185 (77.7%) underwent TKA and 53 (22.3%) underwent UKA. Overall mortality was 35.3% (84/238): 33.5% in TKA versus 41.5% in UKA (OR = 1.41, 95% CI: 0.75-2.63, p = 0.329). Age-stratified mortality showed no significant differences: 80-84 years (31.2% TKA vs. 37.2% UKA, p = 0.467), 85-89 years (42.3% vs. 50.0%, p = 1.000). Multivariable analysis identified age as the only significant mortality predictor (adjusted OR = 1.16 per year, 95% CI: 1.03-1.32, p = 0.013), while implant type was not associated with mortality (adjusted OR = 1.40, 95% CI: 0.72-2.73, p = 0.319). Patient mortality exceeded registry-reported revision rates 3-5 fold.

CONCLUSIONS: In octogenarians, patient mortality substantially exceeds implant revision risk, with no significant difference between UKA and TKA. Surgeons should prioritize patient-specific clinical indications over theoretical implant durability concerns when selecting procedures in this population.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

articles.title: Short- to mid-term clinical outcomes and return to sport and work after arthroscopic debridement of the extensor carpi radialis brevis in patients with chronic lateral epicondylopathy.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to evaluate the short- to mid-term clinical outcomes following arthroscopic extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) debridement in patients with chronic epicondylopathy humeri radialis (cEHR). We hypothesized that arthroscopic ECRB debridement would result in favorable short- to mid-term patient-reported outcomes, improving pain levels, strength, range of motion (ROM) and patient satisfaction.

METHODS: A retrospective case series was conducted on patients who underwent arthroscopic ECRB debridement for cEHR with symptoms > 6 months. Patients were assessed at a minimum of 12 months postoperatively using the Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (DASH) score, and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain. Pre- and postoperative scores were compared using DASH and VAS. Maximum isometric wrist extension strength and postoperative ROM were measured bilaterally. Return to sport and work, patient satisfaction, and complications were documented.

RESULTS: Of the 35 eligible patients, 30 completed follow-up (86% follow-up rate; mean age 48.4 ± 6.6 years; range: 36-65 years; 47% male). The mean duration of symptoms before surgery was 12 months (IQR 8-20, range 6-62). The mean follow-up duration was 28.13 ± 10.9 months (range 12-45). At final follow-up, median outcome scores were 100 (IQR 100-100; range 65-100) for the MEPS, 8.7 (IQR 0.8-13.9; range 0-39.2) for the DASH, 0 (IQR 0-1; range 0-7) for the VAS and 10.3 (IQR 0.8-26.8; 0-79.5) for the PRTEE. In comparison to preoperative values, VAS scores significantly improved (6 [IQR 2.75-7, range 9] vs. 0 [IQR 0-1, range 0-7], p < 0.01), as did DASH scores (46.6 ± 20 vs. 10.3 ± 10.5, p < 0.01). Post-operatively, all patients recovered full range of motion, with an arc of at least 140°. The median wrist extension strength in the operated arm was 98.6% (IQR: 87.4-107%, range: 69.5-121%) when compared to the healthy side, with no significant differences (p = 0.681). Overall, 80% of patients returned to sports at the same or a slightly reduced level, including 12% who achieved a higher activity level than before. The vast majority of patients (97%) successfully returned to their previous professional activities, while only a small proportion (3%) retired from a part-time manual labor position post-surgery, primarily due to age. Furthermore, 83% of patients indicated they would undergo the procedure again. One patient developed posterolateral rotational instability six months after index surgery and consequently required reconstruction of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL).

CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic ECRB debridement for cEHR was associated with improved pain and function and high rates of return to sport and work at short- to mid-term follow-up.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV Retrospective case series.

articles.title: Surgical anatomy of the Over-the-Rectus Extrapelvic (OREX) approach defines safe zones for W-plate fixation of the anterior pelvic ring.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To define the procedure-specific surgical anatomy of the pre-symphyseal region relevant to W-plate fixation by characterizing the soft-tissue layers, identifying critical neurovascular structures, and defining quantitative safe zones for dissection and plate placement.

METHODS: Fresh-frozen adult cadavers underwent standardized low Pfannenstiel dissections reproducing the Over-the-Rectus Extrapelvic (OREX) exposure required for W-plate fixation. Pre-symphyseal soft-tissue layers were sequentially dissected from the skin to the anterior pubic symphysis. The locations of critical neurovascular structures relative to the pubic midline and pubic tubercles were recorded, together with anatomical layers, dimensions of the prepubic ligamentous-aponeurotic complex, soft-tissue thickness, sex-related anatomical differences, and surgical safe zones.

RESULTS: Three reproducible anatomical layers were identified in ten specimens. The superficial layer contained the pre-symphyseal fat pad and superficial epigastric vessels. The intermediate layer contained the spermatic cord or round ligament, ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves, and suprapubic artery, with these critical structures located at a mean distance of approximately 3.2 cm from the midline. The deep layer was consistently formed by the Pyramidalis-anterior pubic Ligament-Adductor longus Complex (PLAC), which covered the anterior pubic symphysis and measured a mean of 4.6 × 3.1 cm. No critical neurovascular structure crossed the central trajectory corresponding to W-plate placement. Female specimens demonstrated greater preperitoneal soft-tissue thickness, whereas lateral surgical safe zones were narrower in male specimens.

CONCLUSION: The pre-symphyseal region demonstrated a reproducible three-layer surgical anatomy with a predictable distribution of critical neurovascular structures. Quantitative anatomic mapping defined procedure-specific safe zones for extrapelvic W-plate fixation and provided practical guidancefor surgical exposure, implant positioning, and avoidance of iatrogenic injury.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, therapeutic study.

articles.title: Risk factors for complications following surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures carries a substantial risk of postoperative complications, particularly surgical site infection, yet the relative contribution of fracture pattern and associated soft tissue injury to this risk remains incompletely defined.

OBJECTIVE: To describe the rate and spectrum of complications following surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures and to identify factors independently associated with these complications, with particular attention to acute surgical site infection.

METHODS: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 126 patients who underwent surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures between December 2014 and November 2024, reported in accordance with the STROBE statement. Candidate demographic, injury-related, and treatment-related exposures were compared against a composite primary outcome (any postoperative complication) and against acute infection using Fisher's exact test, Pearson chi-square test, the Mann-Whitney U test, and multivariable logistic regression.

RESULTS: Overall, 39 of 126 patients (31.0%) experienced at least one postoperative complication; chronic pain (22.2%) and acute surgical site infection (16.7%) were the most frequent individual components. In bivariate analysis, the presence of a Morel-Lavallée lesion at baseline was significantly associated with both the composite outcome (OR 12.65, 95% CI 1.42-112.27, p = 0.011) and acute infection (OR 12.12, 95% CI 2.06-71.37, p = 0.007); Young-Burgess fracture pattern was also associated with infection (p = 0.018). After multivariable adjustment for infection, a Morel-Lavallée lesion (adjusted OR 17.69, 95% CI 2.46-126.95, p = 0.004) and combined-mechanism fracture pattern (adjusted OR 8.25 versus anteroposterior compression, 95% CI 1.91-35.58, p = 0.005) remained independently associated with infection. Neither the presence, technique, nor surgical approach of posterior ring fixation was associated with any complication type, and time from injury to definitive fixation (median 13 days) showed no significant association with either outcome.

CONCLUSION: A Morel-Lavallée lesion identified at initial evaluation was associated with postoperative complications in bivariate analysis and, together with a combined-mechanism fracture pattern, remained an independent predictor of surgical site infection after multivariable adjustment. No statistically significant association was identified between posterior fixation technique and complication risk.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, retrospective cohort study.

articles.title: Aspirin is safe and effective for prevention of deep vein thrombosis following acetabular fracture surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with acetabular fractures are at significant risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet the optimal chemoprophylactic agent remains undefined. Emerging evidence from elective arthroplasty and general orthopaedic trauma populations suggests that aspirin (ASA) may be a safe and effective alternative to traditional anticoagulants. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ASA compared to other anticoagulants for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention following acetabular fracture surgery.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort analysis was performed using a global, web-based health research network that provides on-demand access to de-identified, real-world data from electronic health records and claims. Adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent surgical treatment for acetabular fractures between January 2014 and December 2025 and received VTE prophylaxis within 14 days of surgery were identified. Patients were stratified into ASA (n = 1189) and other anticoagulant (n = 5478) cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to balance baseline characteristics, yielding 1174 patients per cohort. Rates and odds of DVT, emergency department (ED) visits, deep infection, stroke, and readmission were assessed at 14-, 30-, and 90-day postoperative intervals. Temporal trends in VTE prophylaxis utilization were also analyzed.

RESULTS: Compared to other anticoagulants, ASA was associated with significantly lower odds of DVT at 14 days (1.11% vs. 2.22%; odds ratio [OR]: 0.494; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.253-0.967; P = 0.036), 30 days (1.45% vs. 2.73%; OR: 0.524; 95% CI: 0.290-0.950; P = 0.030), and 90 days (2.56% vs. 4.34%; OR: 0.577; 95% CI: 0.365-0.913; P = 0.018). ASA was also associated with significantly lower odds of ED visits at 90 days (OR: 0.741; 95% CI: 0.570-0.963; P = 0.024). There were no significant differences in deep infection, stroke, or readmission rates. ASA utilization increased from 7.2% in 2014-39.5% in 2025.

CONCLUSIONS: ASA is safe and effective for DVT prevention following acetabular fracture surgery and is associated with fewer ED visits compared to other anticoagulants. These findings support the growing adoption of ASA as a VTE prophylactic agent in the acetabular fracture population.

articles.title: Common acetabular fracture patterns in patients with femoroacetabular impingement.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The incidence of acetabular fractures is rising, affecting both younger and elderly patient populations. Developmental abnormalities such as femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and hip dysplasia alter hip biomechanics, potentially predisposing younger patients to fracture. FAI, resulting from a cam and/or pincer deformity, is common, affecting 25% of asymptomatic males and 5% of asymptomatic females, and has been linked to hip pain and early osteoarthritis. However, the relationship between FAI morphology and acetabular fracture pattern remains unclear.

METHODS: Patients, 18-55 years old, treated between 2005 and 2023 for acetabular fracture, hip dislocation, or femoral head fracture were reviewed for FAI morphology using the Judet and Letournel classification systems. Statistical comparisons were conducted using Fisher's exact tests and unpaired t-tests, with significance set at p < 0.05.

RESULTS: A total of 294 patients (72%) exhibited plain radiographic FAI morphology, while 115 (28%) served as controls. The most common fracture pattern in both groups was posterior wall (PW) fractures (23.1% FAI, 31.3% control). Male FAI patients were significantly more likely to experience transverse fractures (p = 0.032, OR=4.6) and posterior column plus PW fractures (p = 0.035, OR=2.5) than controls. Among FAI patients, posterior column fractures were significantly more likely to occur in females (p = 0.011, OR=19). A total of 31 (27.0%) control patients and 63 (21.4%) FAI patients experienced complications.

CONCLUSIONS: In our data set, FAI patients accounted for 72% of patients undergoing acetabular fracture ORIF. FAI patients most commonly sustained posterior wall fractures, but male FAI patients had a significantly higher rate of transverse and posterior column plus PW. FAI patients experienced a complication rate of 21.4% compared to 27.0% in non-FAI patients.

articles.title: Robotic navigation-assisted versus conventional freehand placement of the infra-acetabular screw in acetabular fracture surgery: A retrospective comparative study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The infra-acetabular screw (IAS) is an important component of fixation constructs for complex acetabular fractures, but accurate freehand placement is technically demanding, and evidence on robotic navigation-assisted IAS placement remains limited. This study compared robotic navigation-assisted (RA) and conventional fluoroscopic freehand (CF) IAS placement in acetabular fracture surgery.

METHODS: In this retrospective study, 53 patients with acetabular fractures who underwent IAS fixation between June 2022 and July 2024 were included, 28 underwent RA placement using the HoloSight robotic navigation system and 25 underwent CF placement. The primary outcome was screw-placement accuracy, graded on postoperative CT according to the Lonstein criteria. Secondary outcomes included the number of guide-wire adjustments, fluoroscopy frequency, IAS insertion time, total operative time, intraoperative blood loss, fracture reduction quality, hip function, and complications.

RESULTS: The grade 0 (no cortical penetration) rate was higher in the RA group than in the CF group (96.4% [27/28] vs. 60.0% [15/25], p = 0.005). RA placement was associated with fewer guide-wire adjustments (0.07 ± 0.26 vs. 3.60 ± 1.15), fewer fluoroscopies (9.32 ± 1.66 vs. 21.28 ± 3.18), shorter IAS insertion time (10.36 ± 2.50 vs. 26.68 ± 4.11 min), shorter total operative time (134.54 ± 15.46 vs. 155.80 ± 18.48 min), and less intraoperative blood loss (468.21 ± 84.68 vs. 588.40 ± 80.76 mL) (all p < 0.001). The mean follow-up duration was 15.7 ± 2.0 months (range, 13-22 months). Reduction quality, hip function, and complication rates did not differ significantly between the two groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Robotic navigation-assisted IAS placement was associated with significantly higher screw-placement accuracy and greater procedural efficiency than the conventional freehand technique, without compromising fracture reduction quality, hip function, or safety.

articles.title: The prevalence of mental health service use after long-term minor-to-moderate motor vehicle crash injury: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Minor to moderate motor vehicle crash (MVC) injuries can lead to persistent psychological distress, yet evidence regarding mental health service (MHS) use is limited. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence and characterise the determinants of MHS use after minor to moderate MVC injury.

METHODS: This retrospective cohort study examined Australians with work-related, MVC injuries and workers' compensation claims exceeding 24 months duration. Claims and services data were linked with healthcare records to capture MHS use before and after injury. The injured group was divided into severity sub-groups based on hospital admission status (hospitalised, non-hospitalised). A community comparator group was matched to the non-hospitalised group based on gender and injury year. The primary outcome was MHS period prevalence within 24 months. Determinants of MHS were identified through binomial logistic regression.

RESULTS: There were 574 non-hospitalised, 293 hospitalised, and 8294 community comparators included in the study cohort. The prevalence of MHS use at 24 months post injury was highest for the hospitalised group (36.9%), followed by the non-hospitalised group (31.5%) and community comparators (13.5%). The non-hospitalised group had 3.14 times greater odds (95% CI 2.53, 3.88) of MHS use compared to community comparators, and had the highest prevalence of publicly-funded MHS (18.8%). Hospitalised participants (28.3%) had a higher prevalence of workers' compensation funded MHS compared to non-hospitalised participants (19.3%). The adjusted odds of MHS use were higher among females (OR 2.05 [1.42, 2.97]), and people who had used MHS in the 12 months prior to injury (OR 4.66 [2.41, 9.50]).

CONCLUSION: People with non-hospitalised MVC injuries had a significantly higher prevalence of MHS use compared with their matched community comparator group, and people with hospitalised MVC injuries had the highest prevalence at 24 months-follow up. The highest proportion of people assessing publicly funded MHS was by people in the non-hospitalised group. These findings highlight the ongoing mental health needs of people with minor to moderate MVC injury. Monitoring for the early post injury psychological signs and symptoms, and timely referral to MHS, could reduce psychological burden following MVC injury.

articles.title: Is surgeon technique a modifiable risk factor for heterotopic ossification after posterior acetabular fracture fixation? A multi-surgeon study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Heterotopic ossification (HO) is a well-recognized complication following operative fixation of acetabular fractures through a posterior approach. Established risk factors largely reflect nonmodifiable patient and injury characteristics. Whether surgeon-controlled aspects of operative technique influence HO remains poorly defined. The purpose of this study was to determine if the individual surgeon and specific technique variables are associated with HO after accounting for established patient and injury factors.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 1292 patients who underwent acetabular fracture fixation through a Kocher-Langenbeck approach at two Level 1 trauma centers between 2010 and 2025 by 14 fellowship-trained orthopaedic traumatologists. Patients receiving any form of HO prophylaxis were excluded. Four surgeon-controlled variables were examined: aggressiveness of gluteus minimus debridement, trochanteric osteotomy, thrombin gel use, and closed suction drainage. HO was graded on final radiographs by two independent reviewers using the Brooker classification, with third-reader adjudication for disagreements, and categorized as little-to-no (grade 0-I), moderate (grade II), or severe (grade III-IV). Mixed-effects logistic regression models with surgeon as a random effect were used to assess the associations between patient, injury, and surgeon-controlled technique variables, as well as the individual surgeon, with severe and moderate HO formation.

RESULTS: Little-to-no HO occurred in 1132 patients (87.6%), moderate HO in 96 (7.4%), and severe HO in 64 (5.0%). Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement was not associated with HO severity. For severe HO, the surgeon did not contribute meaningfully to model performance, and no surgeon-controlled technique variables were significant; severe head injury, mechanical ventilation beyond 72 h, African-American race, and dual surgical approaches were associated with severe HO. For moderate HO, the surgeon contributed moderately, and both trochanteric osteotomy (odds ratio [OR] 3.7, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.1-12) and closed suction drainage (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.0-3.1) were associated with increased odds of moderate HO.

CONCLUSION: Severe HO following posterior acetabular fracture fixation is predominantly driven by patient and injury characteristics rather than surgeon technique. Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement does not appear to reduce HO risk, and prevention efforts should prioritize patient-level risk stratification.

articles.title: Association of tranexamic acid with early death or massive transfusion after severe pelvic ring fractures: A nationwide registry-based cohort study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Evidence for tranexamic acid during emergency treatment of severe pelvic ring fractures is limited. We examined its association with early death or massive transfusion.

METHODS: We studied adults in the Japan Trauma Data Bank from 2019 to 2023 with blunt pelvic ring fractures of Abbreviated Injury Scale severity 3 or higher. Exposure was any in-hospital tranexamic acid. The primary outcome was death within 24 h after arrival or transfusion of at least 20 Japanese red blood cell units within 24 h after injury. We used multiple imputation, propensity-score overlap weighting, and hospital-clustered standard errors.

RESULTS: Among 5288 patients, 1985 (37.5%) received tranexamic acid. The weighted primary-outcome risks were 13.0% with tranexamic acid and 18.1% without it (risk ratio 0.72, 95% confidence interval 0.60-0.87). The association was driven by 24-hour mortality (risk ratio 0.62, 95% confidence interval 0.48-0.80); massive transfusion alone (risk ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.73-1.21) and mean red blood cell use did not differ. Any red blood cell transfusion was more frequent with tranexamic acid (risk ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.11-1.30). The primary-outcome risk ratio was 0.76 (0.62-0.93) after excluding deaths within 2 h and 0.81 (0.65-1.00) when both components were assessed within 24 h after injury.

CONCLUSION: The mortality association was not accompanied by lower transfusion requirements and weakened when outcome time origins were aligned. Because treatment timing was unavailable, these findings do not establish an independent survival benefit and provide no corroborating transfusion evidence of a pelvic-specific hemostatic benefit.

articles.title: Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes in patients with severe pelvic ring injury requiring REBOA: A two-center matched cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for life-threatening hemorrhage, but evidence has largely focused on acute outcomes. Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes among survivors treated with REBOA remain poorly characterized.

METHODS: This retrospective two-center matched cohort included 98 adults with severe, hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injuries who survived at least 24 h; hospital survivors required at least 12 months of follow-up. Forty-nine REBOA-treated patients were matched 1:1 to 49 non-REBOA patients by major Young-Burgess category, Injury Severity Score, and age. The primary outcome was functional status among hospital survivors, categorized as good/fair/poor. Deep surgical site infection (SSI) after definitive pelvic fixation was the key secondary outcome, and nonunion was exploratory. Main models used a propensity-score linear predictor based on age, Injury Severity Score, initial systolic blood pressure, and lactate.

RESULTS: Seventy-five patients survived hospitalization (30 REBOA; 45 non-REBOA); median follow-up was 19 months. Good/fair/poor outcomes were 16.7%/46.7%/36.7% in REBOA survivors and 51.1%/37.8%/11.1% in non-REBOA survivors. REBOA exposure was associated with worse functional status after adjustment (common odds ratio [cOR], 3.14; 95% CI, 1.11-8.92; P = 0.032). Among 68 definitive-fixation survivors, deep SSI occurred in 44.0% versus 9.3% (adjusted OR, 7.01; 95% CI, 1.88-31.07; P = 0.003); all observed events occurred within 60 days. Nonunion occurred in 26.7% versus 6.7% (adjusted OR, 9.09; 95% CI, 2.00-53.71; P = 0.004). Sensitivity analyses for deep SSI were directionally consistent.

CONCLUSIONS: Among hospital survivors, REBOA exposure was associated with poorer long-term functional recovery and a higher burden of deep SSI. Nonunion was more frequent but remained exploratory. These findings characterize a high-risk orthopaedic survivor phenotype but do not establish a direct causal effect of REBOA.

articles.title: Impact of sarcopenic obesity phenotype on long-term survival in geriatric trauma: A nationwide cohort study using weight-adjusted waist index.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: As the global population ages, identifying effective prognostic markers for elderly trauma patients has become crucial. While Body Mass Index (BMI) is commonly used, its utility is limited by the "obesity paradox," failing to differentiate between muscle and fat. This study aimed to evaluate the Weight-Adjusted Waist Index (WWI), a surrogate marker for sarcopenic obesity, as a predictor of 20-year mortality following heavy trauma in the elderly.

METHODS: We analyzed a nationwide cohort of 18,366 elderly patients (age≧65) from the National Health Insurance Service-National Sample Cohort (NHIS-NSC) who experienced heavy trauma (hospitalization, surgery, or ICU admission) between 2002 and 2022. Patients were categorized into WWI tertiles. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for 20-year mortality, adjusting for demographics, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and laboratory findings.

RESULTS: During the 20-year follow-up, the highest WWI tertile (T3) was associated with significantly higher mortality compared to the lowest tertile (T1). In the fully adjusted model, the HR for 20-year mortality in the T3 group was 1.72 (95% CI 1.55-1.91). Notably, the risk was more pronounced in obese patients (BMI≧25 kg/m2, HR 2.15) and those with low physical activity. Furthermore, high WWI was associated with a higher prevalence of hip and femur fractures (26.0% vs. 15.0%) and prolonged ICU stays.

CONCLUSIONS: WWI is a superior and independent predictor of long-term mortality compared to BMI in elderly trauma patients. By effectively identifying the high-risk sarcopenic obesity phenotype, WWI provides a practical and powerful tool for risk stratification in geriatric trauma management.

articles.title: Osteoporosis treatment gaps and risk of recurrent hip fracture following initial fragility fracture: Insights from over one million cases.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Patients who sustain a hip fracture are at high risk of a second hip fracture, yet most do not receive osteoporosis pharmacotherapy. We evaluated the association between bone-health medication initiation after a first hip fracture and the risk of a second hip fracture.

METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos, a de-identified multi-institutional electronic health record database. Adults who underwent surgery for a first femoral neck, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric hip fracture were classified as having no bone-health medication, as baseline users (medication documented at admission), or as initiators within six months of the index fracture. Second hip fracture was assessed over fixed 1-, 2- and 5-year horizons. We estimated absolute risks, cumulative incidence accounting for death as a competing risk, and multivariable cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models.

RESULTS: Overall, 1,051,020 patients were eligible for the 5-year analysis: 705,059 (67.1%) had no medication, 83,452 (7.9%) were baseline users and 262,509 (25.0%) initiated medication within six months. Five-year cumulative incidence of second hip fracture was 17.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 17.1-17.3) with no medication, 14.1% (95% CI 13.8-14.4) among baseline users and 8.9% (95% CI 8.8-9.1) among initiators. In adjusted models, the hazard of second hip fracture was lower among baseline users (hazard ratio [HR] 0.71, 95% CI 0.69-0.73) and initiators (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.37-0.39) than among patients with no medication.

CONCLUSIONS: Initiation of bone-health medication within six months of a first hip fracture was associated with a lower risk of a second hip fracture. Baseline users had intermediate risk, which may reflect confounding by indication, agent selection or adherence. These findings support early, coordinated post-fracture osteoporosis treatment; the observational design precludes causal inference.

articles.title: Articular compliance and tolerance to residual incongruity after intra-articular fracture: A hypothesis-driven narrative review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Residual articular incongruity after intra-articular fracture is widely held to cause post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), yet tolerance of a given step-off differs between joints and between regions of the same joint. Reduction targets are nonetheless expressed as uniform millimetre thresholds, and no tissue-level mechanism has been offered for the variation.

HYPOTHESIS: The compliance of the osteochondral unit - cartilage thickness, cartilage material properties and subchondral bone stiffness together - modulates tolerance of residual incongruity, and incongruity is more informatively expressed relative to local cartilage thickness than in absolute millimetres.

METHODS: Narrative review with a documented search of PubMed/MEDLINE (inception to 14 October 2026) covering cartilage and subchondral properties of opposing surfaces, experimental and computational studies of articular incongruity, and clinical studies relating residual displacement to outcome. Four searches returned 3928 records, 3579 after deduplication; 54 sources informed the synthesis. This is not a systematic review; reporting follows SANRA.

FINDINGS: Small, localised contact-stress elevations appear tolerable; step-offs remodel less completely as their height increases; and cumulative contact-stress exposure above a threshold predicts PTOA after tibial plafond fracture. Opposing surfaces differ measurably in cartilage thickness, modulus and subchondral bone thickness, but the direction of the difference reverses between joints and between regions of one joint, so curvature is not a usable proxy for compliance. Clinically, the acetabulum and tibial plafond appear least tolerant, the meniscus-covered tibial plateau more tolerant, and distal radius incongruity predicts radiographic arthrosis more strongly than functional loss.

CONCLUSIONS: The evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, a contribution of osteochondral compliance; joint-level factors confound the clinical data. We set out a Compliance Framework defining measurable determinants, propose relative incongruity as a testable metric, and state four falsifiable predictions with the designs that would test them. Current joint-specific reduction standards should guide practice until those predictions are tested.

articles.title: Lumbopelvic fixation for high-energy sacral fractures and spinopelvic dissociation: A systematic review and meta-analysis of complications, unplanned revision and implant removal.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Secondary procedures after lumbopelvic fixation (LPF) include planned implant removal, removal for symptoms and revision for complications. Their differing indications, together with limited comparative evidence, complicate counselling and surgical planning.

METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched to May 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251036375) for comparative and single-arm studies (≥10 LPF patients). High-energy injuries and fragility fractures were considered separately. Random-effects models summarised complications, unplanned revision, implant removal and within-study comparisons of surgical approaches and fixation strategies.

RESULTS: Twenty-five studies were included (22 high-energy, 3 fragility). Across 19 high-energy LPF cohorts (564 patients), pooled surgical-site infection was 9.3% (95% CI 6.1-14.1), implant loosening or failure was 5.3%, nonunion occurred in 4 of 389 patients (1.0%) and loss of reduction in 2 of 355. Pooled unplanned revision was 11.9% (95% CI 8.7-16.0; prediction interval 5.3-24.3), most often for infection or wound complications. Implant removal was 79.0% in routine-removal series and 17.3% in selective-removal series. Four studies compared minimally invasive and open LPF. Pooling three studies showed less blood loss with minimally invasive LPF (mean difference -271 mL, 95% CI -367 to -175) and shorter operative time (-51 min, -97 to -5); the operative-time association did not persist with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Infection (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.09-1.83) and revision (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.09-1.43) estimates were inconclusive. Four cohorts comparing LPF with posterior pelvic-ring fixation alone reported higher odds of revision after LPF (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.63-9.60), with substantial potential for confounding by indication. Certainty was very low.

CONCLUSIONS: Nonunion and loss of reduction were infrequent after LPF, while unplanned revision most often involved infection or wound complications. Implant removal varied with institutional policy and warrants separate counselling. Minimally invasive LPF was associated with less blood loss, but comparative evidence remains insufficient to establish lower complication rates, equivalent mechanical outcomes or superiority of either fixation strategy.

articles.title: Fracture characteristics in coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus: Clinical significance of medial trochlear involvement.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus exhibit diverse fracture-extension patterns that are not fully characterized by conventional classification systems. The clinical significance of fracture extension into the medial or lateral column remains incompletely understood. This study investigated fracture-extension patterns beyond the conventional Dubberley classification and evaluated their associations with clinical outcomes and bone-related complications.

METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included surgically treated coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus with a minimum follow-up of 12 months at four affiliated institutions between 2012 and 2024. Fractures were classified using the AO/OTA and Dubberley systems. Computed tomography (CT) images were reviewed to assess medial trochlear involvement, lateral column involvement without posterior condylar comminution, and isolated trochlear fractures. Clinical outcomes included elbow range of motion (flexion, extension, and arc of motion) and postoperative complications. Univariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with bone-related complications.

RESULTS: Among 374 surgically treated distal humeral fractures, 35 coronal shear fractures were included in the final analysis. Medial trochlear involvement was identified in 8 fractures (23%) and was most frequently observed in Dubberley type 3 fractures. Patients with medial trochlear involvement had significantly greater loss of elbow extension at final follow-up than those without medial trochlear involvement (-29° vs. -16°, P = 0.042). Bone-related complications were more frequent in fractures with medial trochlear involvement than in those without (50% vs. 7%, P = 0.016). In univariate logistic regression analysis, medial trochlear involvement was significantly associated with bone-related complications (odds ratio, 12.5; 95% confidence interval, 1.69-92.3; P = 0.013). Neither the AO/OTA nor the Dubberley classification was significantly associated with bone-related complications.

CONCLUSIONS: Medial trochlear involvement was significantly associated with greater loss of elbow extension and bone-related complications at final follow-up in coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus. Preoperative CT assessment of medial trochlear involvement may provide clinically useful information complementary to conventional fracture classification systems and may aid surgical planning.

articles.title: Global research on cricket injuries (1982-2025): A bibliometric analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cricket is one of the most widely played sports worldwide and carries a significant burden of musculoskeletal injuries, particularly among fast bowlers. Over the past four decades, research in cricket injury epidemiology, biomechanics, workload monitoring, and surveillance has expanded substantially.

OBJECTIVE: To conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of global cricket injury research, identifying growth trends, influential publications, leading contributors, collaboration networks, and major thematic domains.

METHODS: Publications from 1982 to 2025 were systematically analyzed using bibliometric indicators including annual growth, authorship productivity, institutional and country contributions, citation impact, total link strength (TLS), and co-authorship networks. The top 100 cited papers and the top 10 highly cited papers (HCPs) were examined in detail to identify landmark contributions and research priorities.

RESULTS: A sharp rise in publications occurred after 2003, with nearly 90% of output produced in the last two decades. Australia, the United Kingdom, and South Africa led in productivity, citation impact, and collaborative link strength. The top 10 HCPs accounted for 10% of papers but 37.25% of total citations, underscoring concentrated scholarly influence. Fast bowlers consistently demonstrated the highest injury incidence, particularly lumbar spine and lower limb injuries. Workload spikes were strongly associated with increased injury risk, establishing load monitoring as a central preventive strategy. Biomechanical factors such as mixed bowling action, trunk rotation, and front-knee mechanics were linked to lumbar stress injuries. Standardized injury definitions and international consensus surveillance frameworks significantly improved research quality and comparability.

CONCLUSION: Cricket injury research has evolved into a mature, collaborative, and high-impact domain centered on fast bowling biomechanics, workload regulation, and surveillance standardization. Expanded global participation and integration of advanced analytics are essential for future injury prevention strategies.

articles.title: Machine learning models with SHAP explanations for predicting neurosurgical intervention and six month functional outcome after traumatic brain injury.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Admission information can help describe surgical treatment and subsequent functional outcomes following traumatic brain injury (TBI). We developed interpretable machine learning models to address these two tasks.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 673 adults evaluated at a single center between December 2018 and December 2023. Outcomes recorded were neurosurgical intervention and six-month Glasgow Outcome Scale status, dichotomized as favorable (scores 4-5) or unfavorable (scores 1-3). Patients were randomly allocated to training and internal validation sets in a 7:3 ratio. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select predictors for the XGBoost and random forest models. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, along with classification and prediction error metrics, was employed for model evaluation. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret model predictions.

RESULTS: There were 75 unfavorable outcomes and 66 surgical interventions. The reported validation accuracy for XGBoost was 87.56% for predicting functional outcomes and 95.02% for surgical interventions. Validation Brier scores were 0.083 and 0.035, respectively. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), pupillary light reflex, and blood glucose levels contributed significantly to functional outcome predictions, while GCS, fibrinogen, and white blood cell count were key predictors for surgical interventions. Interpretation of threshold-dependent measures is limited by class imbalance and incomplete specification of outcome coding.

CONCLUSION: The models combined routinely collected admission variables to characterize the treatment received and functional outcomes in a selected traumatic brain injury (TBI) cohort. These findings require confirmation through analysis replication and independent validation before they can be applied clinically.

articles.title: Geography matters: Variations in neck trauma between urban and rural level-II trauma centers.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Geodemographic factors create divergent clinical patterns between urban and rural settings. Level-II trauma centers are a vital trauma-care infrastructure for both urban and rural communities. This study compares neck trauma patterns, resource utilization, and outcomes at these distinct geodemographic nodes.

METHODS: Retrospective analysis (2014-2024) of neck trauma at an urban center (UC, n = 65) and a rural center (RC, n = 60). Demographics, mechanism, treatments, interventions, and outcomes were analyzed.

RESULTS: RC patients sustained more blunt, transport-related multisystem trauma with higher ISS. UC patients predominantly presented with localized penetrating injuries. Rural patients had higher ICU admission rates, longer ICU stays, more transfers to level-I centers yet underwent fewer operative interventions, invasive airway procedures, and CT angiogrophy.

CONCLUSIONS: There are significant variations in neck trauma between urban and rural level-II trauma centers. An "intervention paradox" exists were rural centers stabilize high-severity blunt trauma for transfer, while urban centers provide definitive care for penetrating wounds. These findings necessitate geodemographically tailored protocols. Understanding geodemographic variations is a critical aspect of optimizing trauma systems.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II Retrospective cohort.

articles.title: Synovial fluid biomarker changes after acute anterior cruciate ligament injury: comparison with primary osteoarthritis as a biological comparator.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUNDS: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) typically develops 10-20 years after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but reliable early biomarkers are lacking. We examined synovial fluid biomarker changes in patients with acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group) and in patients with primary OA. The primary OA group served as a biological comparator representing established degenerative OA, not as a healthy or matched control.

METHODS: Our study included patients from January 1, 2021 to September 30, 2023: 51 with primary OA biological comparator and 53 with acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group). Levels of Interleukin (IL)-1β, sulfated glycosaminoglycans (sGAG), aggrecan neoepitope fragment (ARGS-aggrecan), and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) were measured in synovial fluid and compared between the two groups at baseline and one year later. Patients underwent unilateral knee MRI and bilateral weight-bearing radiography at follow-up.

RESULTS: The findings demonstrated that synovial fluid from acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group) and primary OA biological comparator contained inflammatory mediators, collagen markers, and aging-related indicators such as CRP. Following one year of surgical follow-up, PCT, GAG, CTxI, osteocalcin, β-aspartate, and COMP all showed significant decreases. Biomarker comparisons between groups revealed that the primary OA biological comparator had significantly lower levels of CRP, GAG, ARGS, BMP2, FGF-10, and ADAM-TS5 than the ACL-injured (PTOA-risk) group, while CTX-II showed no discernible difference. The Spearman rank correlation was used to examine synovial fluid biomarker concentrations relative to injury duration. Significant time-dependence was observed for: IL-1b (p = 0.025, Rs=-0.112), GAG (p = 0.011, Rs=-0.265), ARGS aggrecan (p = 0.032, Rs=-0.021), C1,2 C (p = 0.002, Rs=0.665), CTxI (p = 0.025, Rs=0.251), C2C (p = 0.011, Rs=0.055), CPII (p = 0.015, Rs=0.336), Osteocalcin (p = 0.029, Rs=0.114), β-aspartate (p = 0.001, Rs=-0.77), D-Asx (p = 0.0215, Rs=-0.425), MMP-3 (p = 0.0201, Rs=0.356), and WOMAC (p = 0.001, Rs=0.264). Univariate regression analysis demonstrated significant associations of IL-1β and osteocalcin with ACL-injured (PTOA-risk) group membership. Multivariate logistic regression revealed significant associations with increased levels of β-aspartate, WOMAC, GAG, IL-1β, and osteocalcin. LASSO regression analysis was employed as an exploratory feature selection method to identify the biomarker panel that best distinguished between the ACL-injured (PTOA-risk) group and primary OA biological comparators within this cohort. Among the 20 variables included in the analysis, five demonstrated non-zero coefficients in the LASSO model: WOMAC, GAG, β-aspartate, IL-1β, and osteocalcin. These findings suggest that inflammatory markers, matrix turnover products, and functional status are prominent features differentiating the acute post-injury state from chronic degenerative OA in this dataset. However, given the exploratory nature of this analysis and the lack of external validation, these results should be interpreted with caution and require confirmation in independent cohorts.

CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate that patients with acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group) exhibit distinct synovial fluid molecular signatures compared with a primary OA biological comparator. These signatures encompass acute inflammatory responses and early matrix remodeling. However, this study cannot explain why only approximately 18.8% of ACL-injured patients later develop PTOA. Future longitudinal studies including ACL-injured non-progressors and age-, sex-, and activity-matched controls are required.

articles.title: Limb preservation and optimization: A whole-patient approach to comprehensive care after catastrophic extremity injuries.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The objective of this study was to describe the Limb Preservation and Optimization Center's (LPOC) components and mechanisms in treating catastrophic extremity injuries and report the initial patient demographics, indications, and outcomes using data from an established registry.

METHODS: A retrospective observational study was performed including all patients entered in the LPOC registry since January 1, 2014. Patient demographics, injury types and treatments, and outcomes, including functional outcomes. Descriptive statistics were calculated to determine proportions, means, standard deviations, and ranges.

RESULTS: 992 patients were included with a mean final follow-up of 20.5 months (SD:22.1, range 0-114); 178 (17.9%) underwent an amputation. Of those who reported RTW, 164 patients (71.6%) reporting RTW at full capacity. Lower extremity injuries were most common (74.9%). Demographic, health insurance, living setting, and presentation variables were similar among LPOC patients. Fractures and soft tissue injuries predominated across all injury categories with fracture fixation and wound coverage treatments most common. Upper extremity joint injuries and all types of combined injuries were associated with the highest reoperation rates. Treatment failure rates ranged from 11% to 100% with fracture and bone-related injuries being associated with the most favorable outcomes across categories.

DISCUSSION: Fractures and soft tissue injuries were the primary types of problems affecting all patients utilizing the LPOC. Fracture fixation and wound coverage treatments were the most performed procedures. Return to the operating room to address the limb preservation and optimization goal was extremely common across categories such that patients may expect at least 4 reoperations. Patients return to some type of work 75-88%. Treatment failure rates varied from 11% to 100%, with fracture and bone-related injuries being associated with the most favorable outcomes across categories. Overall, the results are encouraging and will help shape care in these patients.

articles.title: Epidemiological characteristics and comparison of clinical outcomes between conservative and surgical treatment for rib fractures in South China: A 10‑year retrospective cohort study of 4085 cases with propensity score‑matching analysis.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To systematically describe the epidemiological characteristics of rib fractures in South China and compare the clinical characteristics, hospital stay, and total costs between patients receiving conservative versus surgical treatment, thereby providing evidence‑based support for clinical decision‑making and public health prevention.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on 4085 hospitalized patients with rib fractures admitted to the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Southern Medical University between January 2014 and December 2023. Data on gender, age, injury mechanism, fracture type, complications, blood group, and occupational distribution were collected. A subgroup analysis comparing conservative (n = 586) versus surgical treatment (n = 137) was conducted among 723 patients admitted between January 2021 and December 2023. Propensity score matching was used to balance baseline characteristics between the two groups, and differences in hospital stay, total costs, and injury mechanisms were compared.

RESULTS: (1) Epidemiological characteristics: Of the 4085 patients, 68.13% (2783/4085) were male, and the 41-60 year age group accounted for the highest proportion (50.35%). Autumn and winter were the peak seasons for injury (54.71%). Traffic accidents were the leading cause of injury (51.18%), followed by falls (21.82%) and height‑related falls (19.13%). Multiple fractures predominated (75.52%). The most common complication was pulmonary contusion (45.14%), followed by traumatic pneumothorax/hemothorax/hemopneumothorax/pleural effusion (40.02%). Among occupations, freelancers were the largest group (34.37%), followed by farmers (23.18%). Blood group O was the most prevalent (42.15%), while blood group B was the least common (5.55%, P < 0.001), suggesting that blood group O may be a potential risk factor for rib fractures. (2) Comparison of treatment modalities: The conservative group had a significantly shorter hospital stay than the surgical group [3 (2-6) days vs. 17 (13-26) days, P < 0.001] and significantly lower total costs [5879 (2570-8877) RMB vs. 69,588 (54,499-89,845) RMB, P < 0.001]. The distribution of injury mechanisms differed significantly between the two groups (P < 0.001): the conservative group was mainly injured by falls/slips (44.4%), whereas the surgical group was mainly injured by height‑related falls/ground‑level falls (30.7%). The proportion of concomitant hemopneumothorax was higher in the surgical group than in the conservative group (21.9% vs. 3.4%, P < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Based on a large sample of 4085 cases, this study is the first to systematically delineate the full epidemiological profile of rib fractures in South China, with a sample size more than ten times larger than the previous largest regional report. The results indicate that middle‑aged males, freelancers, and farmers are high‑risk populations, with traffic accidents and multiple fractures being predominant, and a unique autumn peak seasonal pattern in South China is reported for the first time. Treatment strategies should be tailored according to injury mechanism and fracture severity. The novel association between blood group O and increased rib fracture risk, reported here for the first time, provides a new perspective for precision prevention; the potential mechanism may involve impaired hemostatic response due to lower baseline levels of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII in individuals with blood group O.

articles.title: Segmental phase angle as predictor of activities of daily living and muscle health in patients with osteoporotic fracture A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to determine whether the segmental phase angle is associated with clinical outcomes such as activities of daily living (ADL), muscle strength, and skeletal muscle mass in patients with osteoporotic fractures.

METHODS: This was a retrospective cohort study of patients with osteoporotic fractures admitted to convalescent rehabilitation wards. The primary outcome was a Functional Independence Measure motor (FIM-motor) score at discharge, and secondary outcomes were handgrip strength and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI) at discharge. Multivariate analysis was used to adjust for confounders and to examine the association between segmental phase angle and outcome.

RESULTS: A total of 115 subjects (97 women, age 81.0 ± 10.0 years) were included in the study. The median baseline phase angle was 3.6°. Multiple regression analysis adjusted for confounders showed that arm phase angle was independently positively associated with handgrip strength (β=0.250, P < 0.001) and SMI (β=0.215, P < 0.001) at discharge. Leg phase angle was independently positively associated with FIM-motor score (β=0.077, P = 0.045), handgrip strength (β=0.174, P < 0.001), and SMI (β=0.154, P < 0.001) at discharge.

CONCLUSIONS: The leg phase angle was associated with ADL, muscle strength, and skeletal muscle mass in patients with osteoporotic fractures at discharge. Segmental phase angle may be a useful indicator for considering intervention methods in patients with osteoporotic fractures.

articles.title: Union rate and time to union following platelet-rich plasma therapy in fracture nonunion: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fracture nonunion remains a challenging clinical problem associated with prolonged disability and repeated surgical interventions. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been proposed as a biological adjunct to enhance bone healing; however, clinical evidence remains inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of PRP in the management of fracture nonunion.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO Registration: CRD420261366849). PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies evaluating PRP in fracture nonunion and reporting union rate or time to union were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to compare PRP with control interventions. Risk ratios (RR) were calculated for union rates and standardized mean differences (SMD) for time to union. Additional single-arm analyses were performed to estimate pooled outcomes in PRP-treated cohorts.

RESULTS: Twenty-one studies comprising 877 patients were included. Two comparative studies (n = 119) demonstrated a higher likelihood of union with PRP (RR 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-1.36, p < 0.05) without significant heterogeneity. Six studies (n = 250) showed no significant difference in time to union between PRP and control groups (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.48-0.05), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 85%). In PRP-only analyses, the pooled union rate was 0.86 (95% CI 0.76-0.94; I² = 61%) across seven studies (n = 150), and the pooled mean time to union was 6.08 months (95% CI 4.26-7.90; I² = 100%) across eight studies (n = 187).

CONCLUSION: PRP was associated with higher union rates in the limited comparative evidence, although no statistically significant difference in time to union was demonstrated. Heterogeneity in PRP protocols, methodological limitations, and the small comparative evidence base limit the certainty of these findings. PRP may have a potential role as a biological adjunct in fracture nonunion management, but further well-designed randomized controlled trials are required before definitive clinical recommendations can be made.

articles.title: Does greater orthoplastic integration reduce deep infection after open tibial fracture? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Combined orthoplastic management of open tibial fractures is widely recommended, but existing evidence has not quantified whether the degree of care-pathway integration, beyond a binary orthoplastic-versus-orthopaedic distinction, is associated with a graded difference in outcome. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified deep infection and secondary outcome rates across four care-pathway models of increasing team continuity.

METHODS: MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and grey literature were searched in collaboration with a specialist medical librarian. Studies were classified into four care-pathway groups: Group 1, single-setting simultaneous fixation and soft tissue coverage; Group 2, staged care with continuous orthoplastic team involvement; Group 3, discontinuous or delayed plastic surgical involvement; Group 4, purely orthopaedic management. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled deep infection, limb salvage, reoperation, and non-union rates per group. Comparative meta-analyses used genuine within-study comparator arms. Confounding was assessed via meta-regression and subgroup analysis. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and certainty of evidence was rated using GRADE.

RESULTS: Fifty-eight studies (81 classified arms) were included. Pooled deep infection rates rose progressively with decreasing care-pathway integration: 8% (95% CI 5-12%) in Group 1, 16% (9-24%) in Group 2, 28% (11-49%) in Group 3, and 37% (25-50%) in Group 4. A similar gradient was observed for non-union (4-26% across groups). Limb salvage was near-universal (94-99%) and did not discriminate between pathways. Leave-one-out and sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness for Groups 1, 2, and 4; Group 3's estimate was substantially influenced by a single Critical-risk-of-bias study, with deep infection rates attenuating from 28% to 23% on exclusion. No significant publication bias was detected. Certainty of evidence, per GRADE, was Very Low for majority of the pooled estimates, reflecting serious risk of bias and inconsistency, and Low where heterogeneity was minimal.

CONCLUSION: Progressive care-pathway integration is associated with a consistent, graded reduction in deep infection and non-union risk following open tibial fracture, independent of injury mechanism. These findings support continued investment in combined orthoplastic care, including partial integration models where single-setting surgery is not achievable.

articles.title: Province-wide assessment of emergency care capacity and skills in a rural provincial health system: A facility-based cross-sectional assessment in Battambang, Cambodia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Emergency care capacity remains critically limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly in rural areas where specialists and infrastructure are scarce. In Cambodia, stroke and ischemic heart disease are leading causes of mortality, and trauma burdens are increasing alongside rapid infrastructure development. Evidence on emergency equipment availability and frontline provider skills at the facility level in rural provinces remains limited.

METHODS: A facility-based cross-sectional assessment was conducted across all seven public referral hospitals in Battambang Province, Cambodia, in January 2023. Emergency equipment availability was evaluated through structured interviews and direct visual confirmation against the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care. Clinical skill examinations were administered to physicians (two scenario-based cases: acute stroke with airway compromise; traumatic injury with tension pneumothorax and intra-abdominal bleeding) and nurses (a Basic Life Support [BLS] scenario assessed in pairs). Hospitals were stratified by Complementary Package of Activities (CPA) level: CPA1 (basic care only), CPA2 (including surgery and intensive care), and CPA3 (highest provincial level).

RESULTS: At Complementary Package of Activities (CPA)1 (basic care only) hospitals, intubation equipment and 12-lead electrocardiogram were each available in only 25% of facilities. None had a crash cart, blood transfusion capacity, basic metabolic panel, or coagulation testing. In the stroke scenario, airway patency was confirmed by 28.6% of physicians at CPA1 hospitals, compared with 70.0% at CPA2 hospitals (including surgery and intensive care), 57.1% at the CPA3 hospital (highest provincial level), and 75.0% at the Provincial Health Department. In the trauma scenario, no physician at CPA1 hospitals correctly performed spinal immobilization with the spine kept straight or thoracentesis at the correct anatomical location. Among 38 nurse pairs, 97.4% initiated chest compressions promptly, but only 21.1% demonstrated correct compression technique, and 13.2% provided effective bag-valve-mask ventilation. Deficiencies in equipment and clinical skills were most pronounced at CPA1 hospitals.

CONCLUSIONS: Emergency care capacity in Battambang Province was substantially limited, with the greatest deficiencies at CPA1 hospitals. Recurrent low-cost training and targeted strengthening of basic emergency care should be prioritized at lower-level facilities.

articles.title: A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains.

METHODS: This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis.

RESULTS: Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history.

CONCLUSION: ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

articles.title: Early fecal diversion versus no initial diversion in blunt open pelvic fractures: A systematic review and meta-analysis of pelvic infection and mortality.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The benefit of routine early fecal diversion in blunt open pelvic fractures remains uncertain. We examined its association with pelvic infection and short-term mortality.

METHODS: MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 12 August 2026, with citation searching. Comparative observational studies were synthesized using crude risk ratios (RRs), REML random-effects models, modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, and Mantel-Haenszel sensitivity analyses without continuity correction. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed ROBINS-I risk of bias and GRADE certainty.

RESULTS: Eighteen observational comparative reports were retained. Potential cohort overlap prevented a valid unique overall participant total. Eight cohorts contributed to broad pelvic infection (171 participants; seven estimable): RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.35-1.70; I²=19.6%). The stricter outcome-definition analysis included five cohorts (88 participants; four estimable): RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.07-6.97). Excluding two author-reported infected hematomas through an existing replacement sensitivity gave RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.34-2.05). Eight mortality cohorts (236 participants) yielded RR 0.82 (95% CI 0.33-2.07; I²=19.0%). Post-2006 evidence remained inconclusive for infection (three cohorts; RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.009-58.85) and mortality (five cohorts; RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.27-5.26). Diversion was preferentially used in patients with more severe injuries. All reports had Serious or Critical risk of bias; certainty was very low.

CONCLUSIONS: Available evidence does not establish a reduction in pelvic infection or short-term mortality with routine early diversion. Confounding, inconsistent outcome ascertainment, and imprecision prevent causal conclusions or exclusion of benefit in selected high-risk injuries.

articles.title: Enhanced wound healing potential of a carboxymethyl cellulose/gelatin-based hydrogel containing decellularized amniotic membrane and Matricaria chamomilla extract: A multifunctional composite dressing.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic wound healing remains a complex biological process influenced by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial invasion, and insufficient tissue regeneration. Therefore, the design of multifunctional biomaterials that integrate structural support with biological regulation has emerged as a promising strategy in advanced wound care. This study sought to develop a composite hydrogel incorporating decellularized amniotic membrane (dAM)-derived extracellular matrix components alongside Matricaria chamomilla extract, with the goal of achieving enhanced regenerative and therapeutic outcomes.

METHODS: A CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel was prepared using decellularized dAM and subsequently evaluated in terms of its physicochemical and biological characteristics. The effectiveness of the decellularization process and preservation of ECM components were first examined, followed by characterization of hydrogel morphology, rheological properties, swelling and degradation behavior, and pH stability. Its biological performance was further assessed through hemocompatibility, cytocompatibility, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays, as well as a full-thickness wound model.

RESULTS: Incorporation of dAM and chamomile extract resulted in a stable hydrogel with favorable physicochemical and biological characteristics. The decellularization procedure removed 97.9% of the DNA. The resulting composite hydrogel exhibited an average pore size of 78.3 ± 9.8 µm, and all hydrogel formulations showed hemolysis rates below the 5% threshold accepted for blood-contacting biomaterials, with values ranging from 3.8% to 4.5%. The composite hydrogel also supported enhanced fibroblast viability (109.6 ± 11.3%) and demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities against wound-associated pathogens. In vivo, treatment with CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM accelerated wound closure (85.7 ± 6.3% at day 14) and supported tissue regeneration, outperforming both the dAM-containing hydrogel (78.9 ± 9.9%) and the commercial DuoDERM dressing (58.9 ± 4.5%), as evidenced by improved re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and early signs of tissue remodeling.

CONCLUSION: The CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel combines a dAM-containing extracellular matrix scaffold with chamomile-derived bioactive compounds, creating a favorable microenvironment for tissue repair. The addition of chamomile extract to the dAM-containing scaffold was associated with improved wound closure and tissue regeneration. While the present study design does not permit a definitive assessment of synergy between dAM and chamomile, these findings support the potential of this formulation as a multifunctional biomaterial platform for advanced wound healing applications.

articles.title: Can posterolateral tibial plateau fractures be treated with an anterolateral approach? A biomechanical study on novel plating concepts in artificial tibia models.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to evaluate biomechanically whether fixation of posterolateral tibial plateau fractures (PLTPFs) through the more accessible modified anterolateral approach and by using a newly designed lateral plate with or without posterior plate extension or supplemental anteroposterior screw fixation, can provide comparable stability to direct posterolateral buttress plating.

METHODS: PLTPFs were simulated on 40 artificial tibiae and subsequently fixed with 5 different plating techniques (n = 8), namely using Variable Angle Locking Compression Plate (VA-LCP) Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VA Lateral), Variable Angle Optimized Locking Technology (VOLT) Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VOLT Lateral), VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with Posterolateral Extension (Hug), VOLT Posterolateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (PL), and VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with two anteroposterior parallel 3.5 mm locking screws placed superiorly to the plate's lateral-to-medial rafting locking screws (Jail) using a dedicated guide block. Biomechanical testing was performed under progressively increasing cyclic loading to failure. Interfragmentary movements were monitored via motion tracking.

RESULTS: Fragment displacement and its posterior tilt over the first 40,000 cycles did not differ significantly between Hug, PL, and Jail (all p > 0.999). Hug, PL, and Jail outperformed VA Lateral significantly in terms of fragment displacement over 40,000 cycles (p ≤ 0.004). In addition, Hug was associated with significantly less fragment displacement versus VOLT Lateral (p = 0.018). Posterior fragment tilting over 40,000 cycles was significantly lower in Hug, PL, and Jail versus VA Lateral and VOLT Lateral (p ≤ 0.014). Hug, PL, and Jail demonstrated significantly higher cycles to clinical failure and corresponding loads at clinical failure than VA Lateral and VOLT Lateral (p < 0.001), with no significant differences among Hug, PL, and Jail (p > 0.999). For catastrophic failure, Hug demonstrated significantly higher values than all other groups (p ≤ 0.045).

CONCLUSION: From a biomechanical perspective, VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with Posterolateral Extension and VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate with supplemental jail screw fixation provide fixation stability comparable to VOLT Posterolateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with respect to fragment displacement, posterior tilt, and clinical failure. Whether PLTPFs could be addressed via the more accessible anterolateral approach without compromising the biomechanical stability of fracture fixation remains yet to be clinically validated. Standalone Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VA-LCP or VOLT) performed inferiorly to their augmented alternatives.

articles.title: Where is trauma care delivered in New York state? A statewide analysis of distribution and outcomes by trauma center level.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding where and how trauma care is delivered is critical to preventing and managing its disease burden. This study identified patterns in trauma care delivery by characterizing the relationship between trauma presentations and outcomes as a function of trauma center level, including trauma presentations at non-trauma centers.

METHODS: A retrospective review of trauma inpatients aged ≥ 15 years across New York State from 2016 through 2020 was performed, utilizing a comprehensive New York State all-payer data reporting system, the Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS). The primary endpoint for this study was mortality. Secondary endpoints included overall complications, discharge dispositions, and hospital length of stay.

RESULTS: A total of 361,141 patients were included with 42.1% presenting to Level 1 and 37.3% to Non-Trauma Centers. Older adults were more frequently treated at Level 3 and Non-Trauma Centers, while younger patients and high-energy mechanisms (motor vehicle crashes and penetrating injuries) were more commonly managed at Level 1 and Level 2 Centers. The association between trauma-center group and mortality varied by severity of illness (SOI) (interaction p < 0.0001). Compared with Level 3 and Non-Trauma Centers, Level 1 and 2 Centers had higher adjusted mortality odds among hospitalizations with major SOI (aOR 1.43, 95% CI 1.12-1.83) and extreme SOI (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.18-1.62), with no significant difference in moderate SOI (aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.62-1.11).

CONCLUSIONS: Differences in outcomes across trauma center levels are strongly influenced by case mix and severity. These findings highlight opportunities to improve triage, resource allocation, and system-level performance.

articles.title: Variations in hip fracture management at trauma vs. non-trauma centers.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hip fractures represent a growing public health burden. Optimal management relies on timely surgical intervention coordinated by multidisciplinary care and appropriate resource availability, all of which may vary between hospital settings. Differences between trauma hospitals and non-trauma hospitals may influence outcomes, yet these variations have not been well characterized.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of hip fracture cases over a 2-year period (October 2022 to August 2024), comparing patient and procedural characteristics between a Level II trauma hospital (TH) (n = 104) and a non-trauma hospital (NTH) (n = 31). Polytrauma patients were excluded. Data were extracted from the electronic medical record (EMR). Primary outcomes were hospital length of stay (LOS) and time from admission to surgery. Group comparisons utilized chi-square or Fisher's exact tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U or Welch t-tests for continuous variables, as appropriate. A multivariable random forest model was used to evaluate predictors of operative duration.

RESULTS: ASA physical status distribution differed significantly between facilities (p = 0.03), with more ASA > 2 patients at the NTH (76.6% vs. 65.7%). Osteosynthesis was performed in 73.3% of NTH cases and 82.2% of TH cases; arthroplasty comprised 26.7% and 17.8%, respectively. LOS differed significantly by facility (p < 0.01), with a shorter mean stay at the NTH (4.3 vs. 5.9 days; mean difference, -1.73 days). Time to surgery also differed significantly (p < 0.001): mean 846 min (95% CI, 615-1078) at the NTH vs. 2686 minutes (95% CI, 2391-2981) at the TH. In multivariable modeling, procedure type was the dominant predictor of operative duration (permutation importance 0.686), followed by payer type (0.216); facility identity contributed minimally (0.034) after accounting for case mix.

CONCLUSION: Hip fracture care differed meaningfully between the TH and NTH within the same health care system. The NTH demonstrated significantly shorter time to surgery and LOS despite treating a proportionally higher-acuity patient population by ASA classification. These findings highlight opportunities for optimizing timeliness and resource allocation in hip fracture management across hospital settings and questions whether THs are the optimal location to treat these injuries.

articles.title: Comprehensive treatment approaches for traumatic tattoos: An integrative review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Traumatic tattoos result from an injury that drives external pigment into the dermis. They often affect exposed sites such as the face and extremities. Pigment may persist for years within the dermis, complicating management and limiting cosmetic outcomes. Consequently, no optimal treatment technique has been identified, and long-term data remain limited.

AIM: To synthesise evidence on treatments for traumatic tattoos and to evaluate effectiveness and outcomes over the past 25 years.

DESIGN: Integrative review with narrative synthesis following Whittemore and Knafl's five stages.

DATA SOURCES: An electronic search of PubMed and Scopus was conducted from 2000 to November 2025 to identify original peer-reviewed research focusing on treatments for traumatic tattoos and to evaluate their effectiveness and outcomes.

RESULTS: Twenty-eight articles met the inclusion criteria, representing 27 studies, comprising largely case reports and small series, with one retrospective cohort study. Treatment approaches are grouped into laser-based therapies, acute or delayed mechanical debridement (including hydrosurgery), and other surgical or mechanical methods. Q-switched Nd:YAG, ruby, alexandrite, fractional CO2, and picosecond lasers commonly achieve good to excellent clearance with mostly transient adverse effects. Early debridement within 24 h often prevented or markedly reduced tattooing, whereas delayed intervention was associated with residual pigment.
